Item Name: Glan-Taylor calcite polarizer, 5 mm aperture, in SM05PM5 mount on a graduated rotation mount
Part Number: GT5  (no coating suffix on the label - i.e. UNCOATED calcite)  |  mount: SM05PM5
Wavelength Range: Uncoated calcite Glan-Taylor: Thorlabs quotes roughly 350-2300 nm for the uncoated GT series - the widest band of any polarizer in this collection. Uncoated also means ~4% Fresnel loss per surface. VERIFY the exact range on the Thorlabs datasheet before relying on the edges.
Aperture / Size: 5.0 mm clear aperture (the '5' in GT5); SM05-threaded housing seated in a 360 deg graduated rotation mount
Focal Length / Key Spec: Extinction ratio typically >100,000:1 (Thorlabs GT-series spec). Air-spaced calcite prism pair.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): A Glan-Taylor is an air-spaced calcite prism pair: the p-polarised beam passes straight through, while the s-polarised (ordinary) ray strikes the internal air gap beyond its critical angle and is rejected out the SIDE of the housing. Two consequences matter. FIRST, extinction of order 100,000:1 - orders of magnitude beyond any film polarizer here. This is what you use when the polarisation state has to be genuinely clean: defining the input state for an SPDC source, or analysing one in a Bell-type measurement, where a leaky polarizer shows up directly as reduced visibility. SECOND, the rejected beam is dumped INSIDE the housing rather than exiting as a usable port, so it turns into heat. Damage thresholds are low compared with a beamsplitter cube - do not use one as a variable attenuator on a high-power beam, and never on the 532 nm module at full output without checking the rating. MOUNT DETAIL WORTH USING: the SM05PM5 barrel is engraved 'TRANS AXIS' with an index line, and that line marks the TRANSMISSION axis. Zero the rotation dial against it once and write the offset down - otherwise every angle you record later is relative to nothing. Unit A of a matched pair (see the other GT5 row); two high-extinction polarizers is exactly what a two-arm polarisation measurement needs.

Wavelength Range: Uncoated calcite Glan-Taylor, roughly 350-2300 nm per Thorlabs' uncoated GT series. VERIFY on the datasheet.
Aperture / Size: 10.0 mm clear aperture - double the GT5s, four times the area. Bare cubic housing, no mount fitted.
Focal Length / Key Spec: Extinction ratio typically >100,000:1 (Thorlabs GT-series spec). Air-spaced calcite prism pair.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): A Glan-Taylor is an air-spaced calcite prism pair: the p-polarised beam passes straight through, while the s-polarised (ordinary) ray strikes the internal air gap beyond its critical angle and is rejected out the SIDE of the housing. Two consequences matter. FIRST, extinction of order 100,000:1 - orders of magnitude beyond any film polarizer here. This is what you use when the polarisation state has to be genuinely clean: defining the input state for an SPDC source, or analysing one in a Bell-type measurement, where a leaky polarizer shows up directly as reduced visibility. SECOND, the rejected beam is dumped INSIDE the housing rather than exiting as a usable port, so it turns into heat. Damage thresholds are low compared with a beamsplitter cube - do not use one as a variable attenuator on a high-power beam, and never on the 532 nm module at full output without checking the rating. THIS IS THE BIG-APERTURE ONE: reach for it when a beam is too wide for the 5 mm GT5s, which is easy to hit after any beam expander. FLAG: it is unmounted. It needs an SM1PM10 or equivalent holder, and when you fit one you must index the engraved 'POLARIZATION AXIS' mark to the mount's own scale - the engraving is the only reference the crystal gives you.

Item Name: LINEAR FILM POLARIZER, 1050-1700 nm, O1 inch, in a Thorlabs rotation mount - NOW IDENTIFIED
Part Number: LPIREA100-C  (from the printed label kept with it)
Wavelength Range: 1050-1700 nm. That covers 1064 nm AND the whole 1550 nm telecom band - and nothing in the visible.
Aperture / Size: O1 inch (25.4 mm), 3.7 mm thick, clear aperture >90% of the diameter (about O22.9 mm). UNMOUNTED optic, dropped into an SM1 bore in a Thorlabs 360 degree graduated rotation mount.
Focal Length / Key Spec: Extinction ratio >1000:1 (1050-1400 nm) and >2000:1 (1400-1700 nm). Transmission about 45% for unpolarised input. Damage threshold only 1 W/cm CW at 1542 nm and 0.25 J/cm2 pulsed (10 ns) - LOW.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): RESOLVED - this was the "UNIDENTIFIED copper-coloured optic, ON HOLD" row. The printed label identifies it as a Thorlabs LPIREA100-C. MY EARLIER GUESS WAS WRONG IN THE DETAIL: I proposed a wire-grid polarizer. It is not. It is an ABSORPTIVE DICHROIC POLYMER FILM laminated between two AR-coated N-BK7 windows (Thorlabs "Economy Film Polarizers with Windows"). The polarisation function was the right call; the mechanism was not. WHY IT LOOKS COPPER: the AR coating is optimised for 1050-1700 nm, so in the visible it is far off-band and reflects a few percent with the residual peaking toward the red - the same reason 1064 and 1550 nm AR-coated optics look purple-to-copper while visible AR looks blue-magenta. The IR film underneath absorbs most of the visible, so there is no white backscatter to wash the colour out. That coppery flash is a reliable visual tell for an IR-coated optic. NAMING: "LPIREA" = film polarizer, IR, with AR-coated windows (LPIRE without the A has uncoated windows and a narrower 1100-1630 nm spec). The "-C" is the Thorlabs coating band code for 1050-1700 nm. FOUR HANDLING POINTS THAT MATTER: (1) IT IS ABSORPTIVE, NOT REFLECTIVE - the rejected polarisation becomes HEAT IN THE FILM. The damage threshold is only 1 W/cm CW, which is low. Do not put it in front of an EDFA output (MAJ-005, MAJ-010) or any amplified 1550 nm beam without attenuating first. (2) Set the TRANSMISSION AXIS by the mark on the edge of the optic, not by which face points at the beam - the construction is symmetric. (3) COLLIMATED LIGHT ONLY. Do not put it in a converging beam: 3.7 mm of glass plus an angle-dependent film adds aberration and degrades extinction. Designed for near-normal incidence. (4) DO NOT MOUNT IT WITH SETSCREWS OR OVERTIGHTEN THE RETAINING RING - stress-induced birefringence in the epoxy and film wrecks the extinction ratio. A stress-free retaining ring is the right fix. IN CONTEXT: this is the ONLY polarizer in the catalogue that works at 1550 nm. POL-001/002/003 are Glan-Taylor calcite and POL-005 is a visible film polarizer (500-720 nm), so for the telecom bench this is the one.

Notes (Function & Operating Range): RE-READ AFTER THE SETUP CORRECTION. On a 1064-excited, 1550-emitting PL bench this is THE EMISSION FILTER, and the single most important filter on the setup. It sits in front of the detector and does the one job PL detection depends on: block the excitation, pass the emission. Item Name: Ruled diffraction grating, 600 lines/mm, 1600 nm blaze
Part Number: GR25-0616   |   'Grating, Ruled, 600/mm, 1600nm Blaze, 25X25X6mm'   |   TP01066171/T0401307, INSP 445
Wavelength Range: Blazed at 1600 nm - peak efficiency sits essentially on your 1550 nm PL band. Ruled gratings are efficient near the blaze and fall away from it; this one is chosen for the NIR, not the visible.
Aperture / Size: 25 x 25 x 6 mm ruled grating on a substrate
Focal Length / Key Spec: 600 grooves/mm, so groove spacing d = 1667 nm. Blaze wavelength 1600 nm.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THIS PLUS THE SLIT IS A NIR SPECTROMETER, and the rest of the parts are already in this catalogue. Here is the arithmetic that shows it works. At 600 g/mm, d = 1/600 mm = 1667 nm. At 1550 nm in Littrow (incident and diffracted along the same path), 2 d sin(theta) = lambda gives theta = 27.7 degrees. The angular dispersion there is dbeta/dlambda = 1/(d cos beta) = 6.8e-4 rad per nm. Put a 150 mm camera lens after it - you own AC254-150-C (LEN-029), C-coated for exactly this band - and the linear dispersion at the detector is 150 mm x 6.8e-4 = about 100 um per nm. On a 10 um pixel that is roughly 0.1 nm per pixel: a properly sampled NIR spectrum. The 1600 nm blaze is the reason this works well rather than merely working - efficiency peaks right where your PL sits. HANDLING: a ruled grating's surface is a soft replica and CANNOT be cleaned. Never touch it, never wipe it, never blow canned air at it. Handle by the edges and keep it in the case.

Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE SPATIAL FILTER. A pinhole this small is used at the focus of a beam to strip everything but the fundamental spatial mode: the clean central part of the focused spot passes, the aberrated wings do not, and what emerges is a near-perfect Gaussian regardless of how ugly the input was. THE SIZE HAS TO MATCH THE FOCUS, which is where the wavelength comes in: the Airy disc diameter is about 2.44 x lambda x f/D. At 633 nm through a 4.5 mm objective at NA 0.47 (LEN-037/038) the spot is of order 1.6 um, so a 2 um pinhole is well matched. At 1550 nm the same optics give a spot roughly 2.4x larger and this pinhole would clip badly - pick a bigger one, or a longer focal length. ALIGNMENT IS THE HARD PART at 2 um: expect to spend real time walking the focus onto it, and use a low-power beam while you do, because a mis-aligned focused beam will happily burn the foil.

Item Name: Annular obstruction target, 50 um central obstruction - NOT A PINHOLE
Part Number: R1DF50   |   box reads '50um/1mm Annular Dark-field precision pinhole'   |   Thorlabs' own product name: 'Annular Obstruction Target, epsilon = 0.05, Ø50 um Obstruction'
Wavelength Range: N/A - a mechanical/patterned target.
Aperture / Size: Ø50 um opaque central obstruction on a 1 mm clear aperture; obstruction ratio epsilon = 0.05
Focal Length / Key Spec: BLOCKS the central Ø50 um and passes the surrounding annulus - the exact inverse of a pinhole.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): IMPORTANT CORRECTION, because the box's own wording is misleading. It says 'precision pinhole', but Thorlabs catalogues this as an ANNULAR OBSTRUCTION TARGET, and it does the opposite of what a pinhole does: instead of passing a small central spot and blocking the surround, it BLOCKS a Ø50 um central spot and passes the ring around it. Grab it expecting a spatial filter and you will get essentially zero on-axis transmission and a very confusing ten minutes. WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY FOR: dark-field. Placing an obstruction in a conjugate plane removes the directly-transmitted beam, so only light that has been SCATTERED by the sample reaches the detector - a weakly scattering feature that would be invisible against a bright background becomes a bright spot on a black one. The obstruction ratio epsilon = 0.05 means the blocked disc is 5% of the aperture, which is the small-obstruction regime: high throughput for the scattered light, at the cost of less complete rejection of the direct beam. STORE IT AWAY FROM PIN-001 AND PIN-003 so nobody grabs it as a pinhole.

Item Name: Five AR-COATED but UNLABELLED lenses - part numbers unknown
Part Number: None - no part number on any of the five. One is seated in a black anodised ring mount.
Wavelength Range: COATED, band UNKNOWN. The faces throw strong coloured reflections - green/yellow on two, magenta/blue on the others - so every one of these carries a real AR coating. The colour is the residual reflection, so a GREEN residual means the coating is suppressing red and blue and is likely a visible-band design, while a MAGENTA/BLUE residual usually points to a NIR design. That is a hint, not a measurement.
Aperture / Size: MEASURE - five lenses, roughly O25 mm down to O12 mm; the smallest is fitted in a black ring
Focal Length / Key Spec: UNKNOWN - focal lengths not determined.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE ONE GROUP HERE THAT IS WORTH IDENTIFYING. Unlike the uncoated unknowns, these are good optics - somebody paid for the coating - and they are being wasted as anonymous glass. TELLING THEM APART BY EYE: photograph each face under a white LED at a shallow angle and compare the residual colour against a lens whose coating you DO know (LEN-053 is an A coating, LEN-018 is a C coating, LEN-016 is AB). A match narrows the band immediately. THE RISK OF GUESSING: putting a visible-coated lens into the 1550 nm bench costs you a few percent per surface and adds a ghost; that is survivable. Putting one into a high-power beam because you assumed the wrong damage threshold is not.

Item Name: Zero-order half-wave plate, 1550 nm, in a Thorlabs CRM1 cage rotation mount
Part Number: Optic hand-labelled 'WPH1550' on a white tape tab - so a WPH-series polymer/quartz zero-order HALF-wave plate at 1550 nm. Exact catalogue number NOT determined: WPH05M-1550 is the O1/2 in clear aperture version and WPH10M-1550 the O1 in one. Mount: Thorlabs CRM1.
Wavelength Range: 1550 nm design wavelength. A zero-order waveplate is NARROWBAND by construction: the retardance is exactly half a wave only at 1550 nm and drifts away either side, though far more slowly than a multi-order plate would. It is the right plate for your 1550 NIR PL bench and the wrong one for 810 nm or anything visible.
Aperture / Size: Optic sits well inside the CRM1 bore - the visible aperture is small, roughly O10 mm or less, which points to the O1/2 in WPH05M seated in an adapter rather than a full O1 in WPH10M. Focal Length / Key Spec: HALF-wave (lambda/2) retardance at 1550 nm. Rotating the plate by an angle theta rotates a linear polarisation by 2*theta - so a 45 degree turn of the mount flips the polarisation by 90 degrees.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE FIRST WAVEPLATE IN THIS CATALOGUE - everything polarisation-related so far has been an ANALYSER (the GT5s, the GT10, the LPVIS films). Those only SELECT a polarisation and throw the rest away. A half-wave plate ROTATES it without loss, which is the difference between attenuating your beam and steering its polarisation. THE STANDARD PAIRING: put this waveplate in front of one of your Glan-Taylors (POL-001 / POL-002 / POL-003) and you have a continuously variable, polarisation-clean attenuator - rotate the plate, and the analyser converts the rotation into a smooth intensity change with no change in beam pointing. That is a far better attenuator than an ND wheel for a 1550 nm bench. THE CATCH AT 1550 nm: your Glan-Taylors are UNCOATED calcite quoted to about 2300 nm, so they do work at 1550, but at roughly 4% Fresnel loss per surface. THE MOUNT IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE VALUE: the CRM1 gives a lockable, graduated 360 deg rotation inside a 30 mm cage, so this can go straight onto the same cage rods as ACC-002 and LEN-010 on the 1550 NIR PL bench. CONFIRM which WPH it is before ordering a spare - the O1/2 in and O1 in versions are different part numbers and different money.

Item Name: USAF 1951 three-bar resolution test target, 2 x 2 in glass
Part Number: White label reads 'Newport Corporation'. No catalogue number is visible on the plate. Newport's glass USAF target is RES-1 - LIKELY but NOT CONFIRMED (see notes).
Wavelength Range: N/A - a chrome-on-glass amplitude pattern, not a spectral component. It works at any wavelength the substrate transmits; the glass sets that, roughly 380-2100 nm if it is standard optical glass.
Aperture / Size: 50 x 50 x 1.5 mm (2 x 2 in) plate - matches Newport's RES-1 geometry. Fits a Newport FH-2 / FH-2S filter holder. Surface shows scratches and handling marks; the chrome is soft, so treat the patterned face as the delicate side.
Focal Length / Key Spec: Groups roughly -2 through 7, elements 1-6 - so about 0.25 to 228 line pairs per mm. Newport publishes RES-1 as groups 0-7 (1.00-228.10 lp/mm); the low negative groups on this plate are NOT in that published range, which is one reason the part number is unconfirmed.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): WAS NOT PREVIOUSLY IN THE CATALOGUE - this is a new entry. The only thing close was PIN-002 (R1DF50), which is an annular obstruction target and a completely different object. HOW TO READ IT: spatial frequency in line pairs per mm is 2^(G + (E-1)/6), where G is the group number and E the element. Bar width in micrometres is 500 divided by that. Group 7 element 6 = 228.1 lp/mm = 2.19 um bars; group 6 element 1 = 64 lp/mm = 7.81 um; group 0 element 1 = 1 lp/mm = 500 um. Six elements is exactly one octave, each step a factor of 2^(1/6) = 1.1225. WHAT IT IS FOR IN YOUR LAB: this is how you measure the ACTUAL resolution of an imaging path rather than trusting the objective's NA. Image the target, find the finest group where the three bars are still separately visible, and read off the lp/mm. Compare against the Rayleigh limit 0.61*lambda/NA: your OBJ-002 (60x, NA 0.75) should reach about 2200 lp/mm at 550 nm, far beyond this target - so at 2 um minimum bar width this plate CANNOT characterise your high-NA objectives. It is well matched to low-NA work: OBJ-007 (5x, NA 0.12) resolves about 350 lp/mm, and camera-lens or relay testing sits comfortably inside its range. PIXEL-LIMITED, NOT OPTICS-LIMITED, IS THE USUAL ANSWER: with 2.4 um pixels (CAM-001/002/003) you need at least two pixels per line pair, so the sensor caps you near 200 lp/mm at the sensor plane no matter how good the optics are. That is almost exactly this target's top group, which makes it a good match to your cameras. POSITIVE OR NEGATIVE IS NOT DETERMINED, AND IT MATTERS. Newport's RES-1 is a NEGATIVE: clear bars in an opaque chrome field, for back-lit transmission. If your plate is chrome bars on clear glass it is a POSITIVE and it is NOT an RES-1 - Newport does not currently list a positive glass USAF target. THE TEST TAKES FIVE SECONDS: hold it up to a lamp. If most of the plate blocks the light and the bars glow through, it is negative. If most of it transmits and the bars are dark, it is positive. EQUIVALENTS IF YOU NEED A SECOND ONE: Edmund #38-256 (2 x 2 in negative) and #38-255 (positive) are the same geometry and substrate; Thorlabs R1DS1N / R1DS1P are the O1 in versions, groups 2-7.

Item Name: High-power mounted cold-white LED, 6500 K, in its Thorlabs case
Part Number: MCWHL5  |  S/N M00282702  |  case label dated 8-Jul-13  |  owner tape 'CAO&TANG'. Cable is a Binder M8 lead (binder-connector.de, 315849 printed on the jacket).
Wavelength Range: BROADBAND WHITE, roughly 400-750 nm - correlated colour temperature 6500 K ('cold white'). This is a phosphor-converted white LED, so the spectrum is a blue pump peak near 450 nm plus a broad yellow-green phosphor hump, with a DIP around 480 nm and very little red beyond ~700 nm. It is NOT flat - do not treat it as a calibrated white reference.
Aperture / Size: Emitter is 1 x 1 mm with an 80 degree viewing angle. Finned aluminium heat-sink body, roughly O30 mm x 70 mm; SM1-threaded output face (Thorlabs mounted-LED standard) so it screws straight into SM1 tubes and cage plates.
Focal Length / Key Spec: 800-840 mW minimum output; 1000 mA forward current at 3.2 V forward voltage, so about 3.2 W electrical. Radiant flux density about 24.8 uW/mm2. Typical lifetime 100,000 h.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): IT NEEDS A DRIVER YOU DO NOT APPEAR TO OWN. This is a bare LED head with a Binder M8 lead - there is no driver in the case. It must run from a Thorlabs constant-current LED driver (LEDD1B, DC2200, DC4104 or similar) at 1000 mA. DO NOT connect it to a bench supply in voltage mode: an LED's forward voltage varies with temperature, so a fixed-voltage source lets the current run away and the emitter dies in seconds. Constant current, always. WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY FOR: this is the standard Koehler illumination / epi-fluorescence excitation source for a microscope. It replaces an HBO/XBO arc lamp - no warm-up, no alignment drift, no mercury, instant on/off and clean electronic modulation. THE ADAPTER YOU ALREADY HAVE MATTERS HERE: ACC-005 (the unidentified Zeiss-port adapter) and ACC-001 (the EXFO 810-00022) both couple a light source into a Zeiss epi port. An SM1-threaded LED head is exactly what a third-party LED adapter is built to take, so if ACC-005 turns out to have an SM1 thread rather than a liquid-light-guide receptacle, this LED and that adapter are a matched pair. Worth checking the thread on ACC-005 with this in hand. THE 1 x 1 mm EMITTER IS THE NUMBER THAT SETS EVERYTHING: it is an extended source, not a point, so you cannot collimate it tightly - etendue forbids it. Through a lens of focal length f the beam divergence is roughly 1 mm / f. It is excellent for flooding a field uniformly and poor for anything needing a small spot. PAIRING NOTES FOR YOUR FILTERS: at 6500 K it drives FBP-002 (FBH400-40) only weakly - the blue pump peak sits near 450 nm, above that filter's band. FBP-003 (10LF01 488) sits right on the phosphor dip, so expect low throughput. FLP-001/002 (FEL0450) will pass the phosphor and cut the blue pump, which is a clean way to get a warm broadband source. CASE CONDITION: the head and its cable are in the foam; the second foam cutout in the lid area is empty, so check whether a collimation adapter or a driver originally shipped with it.

Your OBJ-001 to OBJ-010 are all RMS, and the Zeiss (OBJ-017) is RMS too. Mitutoyo parfocal is 95 mm against 45 mm for the biological standard, so these cannot share a turret with the RMS objectives without refocusing on every change.

Item Name: Infinity-corrected objective, 50x, NIR-corrected to 1800 nm
Part Number: Engraved 'M Plan NIR 50 / 0.42 / infinity / 0 / f = 200'; black barrel with a teal/blue band. NOTE: current Mitutoyo catalogues list no series called plain 'M Plan NIR' - only 'M Plan Apo NIR'. The 50X / NA 0.42 combination matches M Plan Apo NIR 50X (P/N 378-825-16/-17) exactly, so this is most likely the same optical design under an older engraving. NOT CONFIRMED from a Mitutoyo document.

Aperture / Size: NA 0.42; M26 x 0.706 thread (26 mm x 36 TPI, JIS B-7141) - NOT RMS. Parfocal length 95 mm. Designed for a 200 mm tube lens. No cover glass ('infinity / 0'). L 78 mm, O34 mm, 350 g.
Focal Length / Key Spec: f = 4.0 mm (200 mm tube / 50x). Working distance 17.0 mm. Resolving power 0.7 um; depth of focus +/-1.6 um.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE SECOND OF YOUR TWO 1550 nm-CAPABLE OBJECTIVES, and the higher magnification one. 17 mm working distance at 50x is excellent. WHY THE NA MATTERS MORE THAN THE MAGNIFICATION FOR PL: magnification only sets image scale - you can change it with the tube lens. NA sets how much light you actually collect, and it is fixed in the glass. At NA 0.42 this collects marginally more than OBJ-015 (NA 0.40), so choose between them on working distance and field, not on brightness. ONE THING TO VERIFY: check the barrel really does read NIR. A Mitutoyo 50X/0.42 marked NIR and a visible M Plan Apo 50X/0.55 are different lenses, and the visible one would be useless on your 1550 bench. The NA is the tell: 0.42 at 50x is the NIR series; 0.55 at 50x is the visible one. THREAD AND PARFOCAL WARNING: M26 x 0.706 is NOT RMS. RMS is 20.32 mm major diameter with the SAME 0.706 mm pitch, which is exactly why the two get confused - they will start to engage and then jam. Your OBJ-001 to OBJ-010 are all RMS, and the Zeiss (OBJ-017) is RMS too. Mitutoyo parfocal is 95 mm against 45 mm for the biological standard, so these cannot share a turret with the RMS objectives without refocusing on every change.

Item Name: Infinity-corrected achromat objective, 40x, cover-glass corrected
Part Number: Engraved 'ZEISS ACHROPLAN 40x / 0,65 / infinity / 0,17'; BLUE band.
Wavelength Range: ACHROMAT - VISIBLE ONLY. Corrected at two wavelengths (typically 486 and 656 nm) with the focus in the green. No NIR correction and no SWIR specification. NOT usable at 1550 nm.
Aperture / Size: NA 0.65 (dry). RMS thread (0.8 in x 36 TPI) - the ORIGINAL Achroplan; the later N-Achroplan is M27 x 0.75, so check yours. Parfocal 45 mm. Field number about 25.
Focal Length / Key Spec: Designed for a 164.5 mm ZEISS tube lens, NOT 200 mm. f = 164.5 / 40 = 4.11 mm. Working distance about 0.55-0.60 mm. REQUIRES A 0.17 mm COVER GLASS.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE ODD ONE OUT IN THIS BATCH, in three ways that all matter. FIRST, THE TUBE LENS: Zeiss infinity optics are designed around 164.5 mm, Mitutoyo around 200 mm. Put this on a 200 mm tube lens and you get 40 x (200/164.5) = 48.6x, not 40x. Put a Mitutoyo 20x on a Zeiss 164.5 mm tube lens and you get 16.45x. The formula is M_actual = M_design x (f_tube_actual / f_tube_design). NA never changes - only the image scale. SECOND, THE COVER GLASS: the '0,17' means it REQUIRES a 0.17 mm coverslip. At NA 0.65 that is not advisory - imaging a bare sample with this objective visibly degrades the image through spherical aberration, and there is no correction collar to compensate. Every Mitutoyo in this batch is the opposite ('infinity / 0', no cover glass), so the two families are not interchangeable on the same sample. THIRD, THE WORKING DISTANCE: about 0.6 mm. It practically touches the coverslip. Nothing fits in between - no filter, no window, no cryostat. Compare OBJ-011 at 34 mm. ALSO NOTE it is 'Achroplan', not 'Plan-Achroplan': field flatness is only partial, so expect the edges to go soft. WHAT IT IS GOOD FOR: conventional coverslipped biological or thin-sample imaging in the visible, at the highest dry NA you own (0.65 beats every Mitutoyo here). It is the wrong tool for anything on an optical bench.

Item Name: Infinity-corrected plan apochromat objective, 20x, ELWD - MAKER NOT CONFIRMED
Manufacturer: Motic (LEADING CANDIDATE - not confirmed; no maker name on the photographed face)
Part Number: Engraved 'PLAN APO / ELWD 20X/0.42 / infinity / 0 / WD=20'; GREEN band. No manufacturer name visible.
Wavelength Range: NOT MARKED. If it is the Motic ELWD PLAN APO, Motic does not publish a wavelength range; a visible-band apochromat is the safe assumption. DO NOT USE IT AT 1550 nm without testing - only OBJ-015 and OBJ-016 are confirmed NIR.
Aperture / Size: NA 0.42. Motic's version uses M26 x 0.706 and no cover glass, matching the engraving. Parfocal length and design tube-lens focal length NOT PUBLISHED by Motic - MEASURE THEM.
Focal Length / Key Spec: Working distance 20 mm (engraved). Design tube-lens focal length NOT ENGRAVED - which is itself the point (see notes). Two knurled rings on the barrel.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): SAME NA AND WORKING DISTANCE AS THE MITUTOYO 20x (OBJ-012/013), DIFFERENT MAKER. The engraving style gives it away: Mitutoyo always engraves the series name and 'f = 200'; this one says 'ELWD' and 'WD=', which Mitutoyo never uses. LEADING CANDIDATE IS MOTIC: they sell, for the PA53MET and PSM1000, an objective whose official name is literally 'ELWD PLAN APO 20X/0.420 (WD=20mm)', P/N 1101001700042, with M26 x 0.706 and no cover glass. The engraving matches character for character, including the unusual 'WD=' form. Their whole ELWD ladder shadows Mitutoyo's: 2X/0.055 WD=34, 5X/0.14 WD=34, 10X/0.28 WD=33.5, 20X/0.42 WD=20, 50X/0.55 WD=13, 100X/0.80 WD=3. NOT CONFIRMED - no maker's name is visible on your unit. RULED OUT: Nikon (their ELWD 20x is 0.45 NA at 8.2 mm WD, and CFI Plan Apo 20x is 0.75/1.0 mm); Olympus (LMPLFLN 20x is 0.40/12 mm, a fluorite not an apo, and Olympus designs for a 180 mm tube lens); Mitutoyo (wrong engraving convention). STILL POSSIBLE: Edmund's house-brand EO M Plan Apo 20X, or one of several Chinese OEMs building to the same M26 / 95 mm ladder. THE ONE MEASUREMENT THAT SETTLES THE FAMILY: parfocal length, shoulder to focal plane. 95 mm means it belongs with the Mitutoyos and expects a 200 mm tube lens. 45 mm means it is a biological objective on a completely different design. Then measure the thread major diameter: about 26 mm is M26, about 20.3 mm is RMS. Thirty seconds with calipers. ON THE TWO KNURLED RINGS: probably NOT a correction collar. An objective engraved 'infinity / 0' is specified for zero cover glass, so a cover-glass collar would be pointless, and a real one carries a graduated range like '0-2' or '0.17-1.1'. More likely a grip knurl, a retaining ring, or an iris diaphragm - some metallurgical apos have one.

Item Name: Near-infrared image-converter viewer (IR viewer) - HANDLE WITH CARE
Part Number: Front label: boxed 'FJW' + 'FIND-R-SCOPE'. Exact model NOT ENGRAVED on the visible face. Body style (grey housing, rubber eyecup, knurled focus ring, separate knurled objective) matches the 84499 / 84499A generation. Owner tape reads '...b Tang lab'.
Wavelength Range: 350-1350 nm for the STANDARD tube, with sensitivity peaks near 350 and 800 nm. THE '-5' VARIANTS (84499C-5 and similar) EXTEND TO 1550 nm - and yours is not marked, so DO NOT ASSUME IT SEES 1550 nm. Even on a -5 tube the 1550 nm response is weak; sellers grade individual tubes as 'strong at 1300, some response at 1550'.
Aperture / Size: Hand-held monocular. Infragon 25 mm f/1.0 objective, about 70 lp/mm, 40 degree field of view, roughly 1:1 magnification. Runs from a single C alkaline cell (250 h intermittent, 375 h continuous).
Focal Length / Key Spec: NOT a thermal imager. An electrostatically-focused IR IMAGE CONVERTER TUBE: photocathode converts NIR photons to electrons, a high-voltage stage accelerates them onto a phosphor screen you view directly. The scene must EMIT or BE ILLUMINATED - it is not a passive thermal camera.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): WHY YOU WERE TOLD TO HANDLE IT CAREFULLY, IN FJW'S OWN WORDS: 'Viewing excessively high powered light may damage the FIND-R-SCOPE image tube.' A focused or specularly reflected laser beam burns a PERMANENT dark spot into the photocathode or phosphor. Tubes are not repairable - only replaceable, and an 84499A listed around $1,695. THE RULE ON A LASER BENCH: view SCATTERED light only. Never look into a direct beam, and never at a specular reflection off a mirror, a lens face or a polished mount. Use an ND or attenuating filter if in any doubt. TWO MORE FROM THE MANUAL: do not rotate the eyepiece past the point of easy movement (it damages the tube), and DO NOT DROP IT - the tube is fragile glass. WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY FOR IN YOUR LAB: finding an invisible beam. Your 810 nm SPDC path (FBP-009) sits near the tube's peak sensitivity, so this is the right tool for aligning that. Your 1064 nm filters (FBP-004/FBP-011) are within range too. BUT AT 1550 nm IT IS PROBABLY BLIND. If you need to see the 1550 NIR PL bench, the right tools are an InGaAs camera or a SWIR viewer (FJW's own 85900 SWIR-View is InGaAs, 400-1700 nm), not this. Your CAM-004 (IDS NIR-enhanced Si) is also capped by silicon at ~1100 nm. MODEL MATTERS IF YOU EVER BUY A TUBE: the 84499 has a FIXED objective and a small tube; the 84499A has a REMOVABLE objective, a black removable eyepiece insert with screws, and a larger tube - and it takes C-mount lenses through an adapter. Check whether your objective unscrews to tell them apart.

Item Name: Auxiliary objective or close-up lens for the Find-R-Scope - MODEL NOT MARKED
Manufacturer: FJW Optical Systems (assumed - photographed with the viewer)
Part Number: No part number visible. Grey textured cylinder with black end caps at both ends.
Wavelength Range: Passive optic - the viewer tube sets the usable band, not this lens.
Aperture / Size: MEASURE - roughly the same diameter as the viewer barrel. Check the thread: FJW close-up lenses use 27 mm and 30.5 mm threads; auxiliary objectives are C-mount.
Focal Length / Key Spec: UNDETERMINED. Most consistent with an AUXILIARY C-MOUNT OBJECTIVE or a CU400 close-up lens stored in its caps.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): PHOTOGRAPHED WITH INS-002 and almost certainly its accessory. FJW's accessory line for the Find-R-Scope includes C-mount auxiliary objectives at 8, 16, 25 and 50 mm, a 12.5-75 mm zoom, CU400 close-up attachments (27 mm and 30.5 mm thread, focusing down to about 2 inches), visible-cut and ND filters, step-up rings and an iris assembly. AN IR ILLUMINATOR IS THE LEAST LIKELY READING - FJW does not prominently catalogue a standalone illuminator in these bulletins. Not disproven, just unsupported. Two lens groups and a C-mount thread means an auxiliary objective; a single element with a 27 or 30.5 mm filter thread means a close-up attachment. Item Name: Large adjustable sample holder on a four-rod cage frame
Manufacturer: Unbranded / unmarked (finish and hardware look Thorlabs-compatible)
Part Number: No part number and no maker mark visible.
Wavelength Range: N/A - mechanical mount.
Aperture / Size: MEASURE - two black anodised plates riding on four polished stainless rods; one plate carries a wide V-groove jaw, the other is flat with two knurled thumbscrews. Rod diameter and spacing NOT MEASURED - that is what decides whether it drops onto your existing 30 mm cage hardware.
Focal Length / Key Spec: Adjustable jaw spacing along the rods, locked by knurled thumbscrews. The V-groove face self-centres a cylindrical or a square sample; the flat face clamps against it.

The V-groove is the useful part: a V self-centres whatever you put in it, so a round sample stays on the same axis whatever its diameter - which is exactly what you want when you swap samples and do not want to realign. MEASURE THE ROD DIAMETER FIRST. 6 mm means it is standard 30 mm cage-system rod (Thorlabs ER series) and it will bolt straight onto the cage hardware you already have on the 1550 NIR PL bench (ACC-002 and LEN-010 are on 30 mm cage rods). 1/4 inch or 12 mm means it is a stand-alone jig. THIS IS THE BIGGEST SAMPLE APERTURE IN THE CATALOGUE. Everything else that holds a sample here is O1 inch or smaller. If you need to put a wafer piece, a cryostat window or a bulk crystal in a beam, this is the only thing you own that will take it. WATCH THE THERMAL PATH: a black anodised aluminium clamp is a decent heat sink, so if you clamp something you are illuminating with LED-001 or a laser, the clamp will pull heat out asymmetrically and can bend the sample. Matters for anything thin.

Item Name: Handheld optical power meter console, 1916-C
Part Number: 'Optical Power Meter - Model 1916-C' printed on the front. Newport lists it as OBSOLETE; the RoHS replacement is the 1916-R, and the current equivalent is the 1919-R.
Wavelength Range: None of its own - set entirely by the detector plugged in. Paired here with the 818-SL (MTR-006): 400-1100 nm.
Aperture / Size: 76 x 57 mm LCD, 2 Hz update. DB-15 female detector input. Runs on 4 x AA alkaline, about 670 h. External 9 VDC jack.
Focal Length / Key Spec: 1 nW to 10 kW depending on the detector. Resolution 1 pW with 818-series photodiodes, 1 mW with most 818P thermopiles. Accepts Newport 818, 918D and 818P heads.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): YOUR THIRD POWER-METER CONSOLE, alongside MTR-001 (Thorlabs PM100) and MTR-003 (Coherent FieldMaxII-TO). They are not interchangeable - each takes its own maker's heads, and each head carries its own calibration. THE ONE REAL LIMITATION: the 1916-C has NO COMPUTER INTERFACE. No USB, no RS232 - only a DC power jack. If you ever need logged power traces you cannot get them from this console; the 1918-C and the current 1919-R add USB, internal memory and on-board statistics. WHAT IT IS GOOD AT: it is a clean, low-noise handheld with 1 pW resolution on a photodiode head, which is far better than anything else you own for weak signals. SEE ALSO MTR-006 (the 818-SL head) and the DET-ADAP-PD adapter on its cable - those two arrived with it and are what make the pairing work.

Item Name: Calibrated silicon photodiode detector head, 818-SL, with BNC-to-DB15 adapter
Part Number: Head label: 'MODEL 818-SL', S/N 8134. Blue cable terminating in a D-sub shell marked 'DET-ADAP-PD'.
Wavelength Range: 400-1100 nm (silicon). DOES NOT REACH 1550 nm - silicon's response dies past about 1100 nm, and the head is uncalibrated and effectively blind there. Same limitation as MTR-002 (Thorlabs S130A) and MTR-004 (PM16-121).
Aperture / Size: Sensor O11.3 mm; clear aperture O10.3 mm - the largest photodiode aperture in your collection. Round black puck head.
Focal Length / Key Spec: 20 pW to 2 W WITH the removable OD3 attenuator fitted. Take the attenuator off for low-power work and the useful ceiling drops to the low-mW range, with a 20 pW floor. 'SL' means Silicon, Low-power.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): KEEP THE ATTENUATOR WITH THE HEAD. The calibration certificate ties the ATTENUATOR serial number to the DETECTOR serial number - they are calibrated as a pair. Mix attenuators between heads and every reading is wrong by an unknown factor, silently. THE THREE-DECADE TRICK: the OD3 attenuator is what buys this head its 20 pW to 2 W span. Fitted, you can measure a 1 W beam; removed, you can measure picowatts. Remember which state it is in before trusting a number. WHAT THE BLUE CABLE'S ADAPTER IS: DET-ADAP-PD is Newport's BNC-to-DB15 adapter. This is a legacy BNC-output 818 head, and the 1916-C (MTR-005) has a DB-15 input - the adapter is what mates them. That is why the console, the head and the adapter all turned up together. FOR YOUR 1550 nm BENCH YOU NEED A DIFFERENT HEAD: none of your four photodiode detectors reaches 1550 nm. The right part is a Newport 818-IG (InGaAs, 800-1650 nm) or 818-IR (germanium, 780-1800 nm), and the 818-IG is the better choice at 1550. Both plug into this same 1916-C console. THIS IS A REAL GAP IN THE LAB: you have a 1550 nm laser (LSR-002), NIR objectives (OBJ-015/016), C-coated optics and NIR filters - and NO WAY TO MEASURE POWER at that wavelength.

Item Name: Air-cooled thermopile laser power sensor head - MODEL NOT CONFIRMED
Part Number: No model number visible in the photo. Form - a black anodised finned disc with an axial aperture and a side-exiting cable - is the Coherent PowerMax air-cooled family. On size (about 50-60 mm outer diameter) the closest catalogue match is the PM30 (O63 mm, 100 mW - 30 W); the PM10 (10 mW - 10 W) is the other strong candidate and Coherent sold a stock FieldMaxII-TO + PM10 kit. NOT CONFIRMED - read the model off the head or off the console's sensor-ID screen.
Wavelength Range: 0.25 to 11 um - essentially wavelength-INDEPENDENT. A thermopile absorbs the light as heat and reads the temperature gradient, so response is flat from the UV to the CO2 line, unlike a photodiode whose responsivity varies steeply and dies at the bandgap.
Aperture / Size: Finned black convection heat sink, roughly 50-60 mm across. Aperture 19 mm on both candidate models. Mounted here on a Thorlabs post clamp. DB-25 SmartProbe connector - the head carries its own calibration data, so the console auto-identifies it.
Focal Length / Key Spec: PM30: 100 mW - 30 W. PM10: 10 mW - 10 W (30 W for under 5 min). Damage threshold 6 kW/cm2 on both. The console was photographed reading 3.34 W, which sits comfortably mid-scale either way.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THIS IS THE HEAD THAT GOES WITH MTR-003 (the Coherent FieldMaxII-TO console) - the pair is your ONLY high-power capability. Every other detector you own is a photodiode: MTR-002 tops out at 500 mW, MTR-004 at 500 mW, MTR-006 at 2 W. A 3.34 W beam would saturate or destroy any of them. WHY A THERMOPILE IS THE RIGHT INSTRUMENT HERE, AND THE TRADE: you can change wavelength - 532, 1064, 1550 nm, anything - and the reading stays valid with only a small percent-level wavelength-correction entry on the console. No detector swap, no recalibration. That is the opposite of your photodiode heads, which each cover one band and none of which reach 1550 nm. THE PRICE YOU PAY IS SPEED AND FLOOR: a thermopile has a thermal time constant of seconds. LET THE READING SETTLE before believing it - an unsettled thermopile reads low and drifts upward, which looks exactly like a laser warming up. And below roughly 10-100 mW it is useless; go back to a photodiode there. THE NUMBER THAT ACTUALLY DAMAGES IT IS POWER DENSITY, NOT POWER: the limit is 6 kW/cm2. Spread over the 19 mm aperture, 3.34 W is nothing. FOCUSED to a 100 um spot, under a watt already exceeds the threshold. Keep the beam unfocused, roughly centred, and filling a sensible fraction of the aperture. IT IS BEING USED AS A BEAM DUMP TOO: in the photo it sits directly in front of a laser aperture, which is exactly right - the finned body is designed to convect that heat away. Do not put it in a closed box.

Item Name: Ordinary tinted sunglasses - NOT LASER EYEWEAR
Part Number: Lens marking reads '...UV400 CAT.3 EN ISO 12312-1' (partially obscured). One purple frame, one black/blue frame.
Wavelength Range: UV400 means it blocks to 400 nm. CAT.3 is a SUN-GLARE category (roughly 8-18% visible transmittance). THERE IS NO OPTICAL DENSITY RATING AT ANY WAVELENGTH.
Aperture / Size: Standard sunglass frames, no side shields.
Focal Length / Key Spec: NOT a laser rating. EN ISO 12312-1 is the SUNGLASSES standard. Laser eyewear is certified to EN 207 (direct beam, LB rating) or EN 208 (alignment, RB rating). This carries neither.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THESE ARE SUNGLASSES, NOT SAFETY EQUIPMENT. Recorded here only so nobody mistakes them for laser goggles - they were photographed with the real eyewear and they look the part on a bench. WHY THE 'UV400' MARKING IS ACTIVELY MISLEADING IN A LASER LAB: it means the lens attenuates below 400 nm to a consumer standard, which is unquantified in OD terms and is typically only around OD 1-2. Your LSR-003 is a 100 mW 405 nm CUBE - just above that cut-off anyway - and 100 mW through OD 2 is still 1 mW hitting the retina, a thousand times a safe exposure. A CAT.3 TINT MAKES THINGS WORSE, NOT BETTER, in one specific way: it is dark enough to dilate your pupil, so if a beam does get through you take MORE of it than with no glasses at all. USE THEM OUTDOORS. Do not let them near a running laser.

Item Name: UV-blocking safety spectacles - explicitly NOT laser rated
Part Number: No manufacturer marking visible. A hand-applied label on the temple reads 'UV only!  NO LASER'.
Wavelength Range: UV blocking only. No optical density figure and no wavelength band is marked anywhere on the lens.
Aperture / Size: Wraparound grey-tinted lens with integrated side shields; wide fit, can go over prescription glasses.
Focal Length / Key Spec: NOT laser rated - somebody in the lab has already labelled them so, which is exactly the right thing to have done.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): SOMEBODY ALREADY DID THE IMPORTANT WORK HERE and stuck a label on them. Keep that label on. WHAT THEY ARE ACTUALLY FOR: UV lamp work, a UV curing box, or handling anything under a blacklight - the classic case where you need broadband UV protection but no laser rating. The side shields matter for that job, because UV scattered off a bench reaches your eyes from the side. WHY THEY ARE NOT ENOUGH FOR A LASER: a UV filter has no specified optical density at a specific line, and it cannot survive a direct beam - EN 207 laser eyewear is tested to withstand a direct hit for 10 seconds without burning through. A UV lens is not. THE ONE UV SOURCE IN THIS CATALOGUE that this genuinely suits is nothing laser-based; your 405 nm CUBE (LSR-003) is a LASER and needs SAF-006 instead.

Item Name: Laser safety goggles - UV + NIR, amber lens, 25% VLT
Part Number: 'NOIR' and CE marked on the lens. Left lens: '180-400nm OD 6+  720-1090nm OD 5+  750-1064nm OD 7+   25% VLT'. Right lens (EN 207 scale numbers): '180-315 D LB6 + R LB4 / >315-400 DR LB4 / 720-725 DM LB5 / 720-750 + >1064-1075 IR LB5 / >725-1075 DM LB6 / >750-1064 IR LB7'.
Wavelength Range: BLOCKS: 180-400 nm at OD 6+, 720-1090 nm at OD 5+, and 750-1064 nm at OD 7+. PASSES: the whole visible band from 400 to 720 nm. That is deliberate - it is what makes them wearable - but it means they give you NOTHING at 405, 532 or 633 nm.
Aperture / Size: Wraparound frame with side protection; amber/yellow lens. 25% visible light transmission, so the bench stays usable.
Focal Length / Key Spec: OD 7+ at 750-1064 nm is the deepest protection in your collection - attenuation by a factor of ten million.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE ONE FOR YOUR SPDC AND 1064 nm WORK. 810 nm (FBP-009, the degenerate SPDC line) sits at OD 5+, and 1064 nm (FBP-004, FBP-011) at OD 7+. READ THE UV BAND CAREFULLY - IT STOPS AT 400 nm. Your 405 nm CUBE (LSR-003) is 5 nm OUTSIDE the protected band. These goggles do NOT protect you from it. That is a trap, because 'UV protection' plus a violet laser feels like it should match. It does not. WHAT THE EN 207 CODES MEAN: LB6 means the lens survives a direct beam and attenuates by 10^6; D is continuous wave, I and R are pulsed and giant-pulse regimes, M is mode-locked. So 'IR LB7' at 750-1064 nm means it is rated for a pulsed IR beam at OD 7. This is a REAL EN 207 rating - unlike SAF-001 and SAF-002, this lens is tested to take a direct hit without burning through. 25% VLT IS THE PRACTICAL VIRTUE: dark enough to be safe in its bands, light enough that you can still see the bench and your samples. Compare the green NIR goggles (SAF-004/005), which are far harder to work in.

Item Name: Laser safety goggles - NIR / Nd:YAG, green lens
Part Number: Left lens: '800-1100nm OD5+  1060-1070nm OD7+'. Right lens: '800-1100nm DIR LB5 / 1000-1070nm IR LB7 LP S' + CE.
Wavelength Range: BLOCKS: 800-1100 nm at OD 5+, with a deeper OD 7+ notch at 1060-1070 nm (the Nd:YAG line). PASSES: everything below 800 nm. NO protection at 405, 532 or 633 nm, and none at 1550 nm.
Aperture / Size: Wraparound frame with side protection; green lens.
Focal Length / Key Spec: OD 7+ at 1060-1070 nm - built specifically around the 1064 nm Nd:YAG fundamental.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): BUILT FOR A 1064 nm LASER. The deep notch at 1060-1070 nm is the giveaway; the broader 800-1100 nm OD 5+ band covers the rest of the NIR including your 810 nm SPDC line. THE DANGEROUS CASE THIS DOES NOT COVER: a frequency-doubled Nd:YAG leaks 532 nm as well as 1064 nm, and these goggles pass 532 nm completely. Your LSR-001 is a 532 nm DPSS at 200 mW built on exactly that chain. If you are ever working on both at once, these are not enough on their own. COMPARE SAF-003: the NoIR amber gives you 750-1064 nm at OD 7+ AND the UV band, at 25% VLT. These greens give a deeper, narrower Nd:YAG notch. For 1064 nm work either is fine; for mixed 810 and UV work the amber is the better single choice.

Item Name: Laser safety goggles - NIR, green lens (second pattern)
Part Number: Left lens: '800-900nm OD>6  900-1100nm OD>7'. Right lens: '800-900nm D LB5 + IR LB7 / >900-1080nm D LB5 + IR LB7 LP' + CE.
Wavelength Range: BLOCKS: 800-900 nm at OD >6 and 900-1100 nm at OD >7. PASSES: everything below 800 nm, and everything above 1100 nm - so NOTHING at 405, 532, 633 or 1550 nm.
Aperture / Size: Wraparound frame with side protection; green lens. Photographed as a stack of at least two identical pairs.
Focal Length / Key Spec: OD >7 across the whole 900-1100 nm span - broader deep protection than SAF-004, which only reaches OD 7+ in the narrow 1060-1070 nm notch.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE BEST PURE-NIR PROTECTION YOU OWN: OD >6 from 800 nm and OD >7 from 900 to 1100 nm, so both your 810 nm SPDC line and the 1064 nm Nd:YAG line are deeply covered by one lens without relying on a narrow notch. QUANTITY IS UNCERTAIN - the photo shows a stack and at least two pairs carry this exact marking. Recorded as 2; count them properly and correct it. SAME BLIND SPOTS AS SAF-004: nothing in the visible, nothing at 1550 nm. GREEN LENSES ARE HARD TO WORK IN. They pass a narrow green window, which is why the bench looks green and why colour-coded wiring and indicator LEDs become unreadable. That is a real practical hazard of its own - people take goggles off to read a label. Keep the amber SAF-003 available for jobs where you must see properly.

Item Name: Laser safety goggles - UV / violet / green, red lens

Part Number: Green-and-white label: 'Line Tool Co. / 943 Kurtz St / Allentown, PA'. Model plate reads 'Model  A  LH'. Starrett micrometer heads.

Notes (Function & Operating Range): Line Tool Company, 943 Kurtz St, Allentown PA - family-owned since 1954 and STILL IN BUSINESS, making micropositioners and nothing else. WAYS ARE BALL-RACE, NOT DOVETAIL: hardened tool-steel slides and ball races at 60-62 Rc, nickel plated, in a cast aluminium body with enamel finish. These are the classic semiconductor probe-station positioners - probe-station vendors still list a 'Line Tool Series'. 'LH' MEANS LEFT-HAND - a mirror-image build, so the micrometer barrels come out on the opposite side from an RH unit. THAT IS NOT COSMETIC. Matched LH and RH pairs are how you work a sample from both sides without the knobs colliding, and how you keep both operators' controls facing outward. If you ever buy a partner for this one, buy the RH. HOW THEY COMPARE WITH YOUR NEWPORT 462s (STG-001/002/003): the Newports are crossed-roller, individually tested to under 100 urad, and take a 191 N load. Line Tool publishes no straightness or angular figures at all, and a ball-race slide of this vintage will show more stick-slip, more angular wander and less stiffness. Resolution is limited by the micrometer graduation, not by a fine drive. USE THEM FOR WHAT THEY ARE GOOD AT: coarse-to-medium positioning of a probe, a fibre or a detector where a few microns is fine and you want a knob you can turn by feel. Use the Newports where angular deviation matters - anything in a beam path where tilt turns into pointing error.

WHAT THE 'ESP COMPATIBLE' STICKER MEANS: ESP is Newport's plug-and-play stage-recognition scheme (documented as 'Enhanced System Performance', later marketed as 'Embedded Stage Parameters'). On power-up the controller reads the stage's identity down the cable and auto-loads travel limits, encoder resolution, max velocity and acceleration, servo gains and home-search parameters. You plug it in and it works. CONTROLLERS THAT CAN READ IT: XPS-D and XPS-RLD (current), ESP302 (current), SMC100CC for DC or SMC100PP for stepper (current), ESP301 (DISCONTINUED September 2020), ESP300 (long obsolete). WHAT YOU LOSE GOING GENERIC: the auto-configuration, Newport's factory-tuned servo gains, and you must derive counts-per-mm and work out limit-switch polarity and supply voltage yourself. Get the limits wrong and the carriage drives into a hard stop. THE WARNING ON THE LABEL IS REAL: 'Do not connect or disconnect while power is applied.' Hot-plugging the DB-25 can destroy the driver output stage. THE DB-25 CARRIES EVERYTHING on one connector - motor phases or DC motor leads, encoder A/B/index differential pairs, positive and negative limit inputs, home signal, and the stage-ID lines. Pin mapping is in Appendix C of the ESP300 / ESP301 manual - pull it and buzz the connector out before wiring anything yourself. MIXING THESE WITH YOUR NEWMARK STAGES: no single controller runs both plug-and-play. The Newport CC stages are BRUSH DC SERVO; STG-016, STG-017 and STG-018 are NEMA-17 two-phase STEPPERS. SMC100CC is DC-only and SMC100PP is stepper-only. An ESP302 or an XPS-D with mixed driver modules is the only single box that can do both - and even then the Newmark axes get no ESP identification and must be configured by hand, with a custom adapter harness because Newmark splits motor and signals across separate connectors. THE SENSIBLE SPLIT: Newport stages on an ESP302, Newmark stages on the NSC-A1 family, coordinated in software (Python, LabVIEW or MATLAB) rather than forcing one controller. HISTORY: Newport bought Micro-Controle's micro-positioning division in 1991 for $43 million. The French operation continued as Micro-Controle Spectra-Physics S.A. in Evry and still builds the ILS, IMS, UTS and MTM lines - which is why current Newport stages say 'Made in France'.

Item Name: HIGH-SPEED NIR photoreceiver, 22 GHz - for optical communications - LINEAR, NOT a photon counter
Manufacturer: New Focus (now a Newport brand within MKS Instruments)
Part Number: Front panel: 'Model 1484-A-50 / 22-GHz NIR Photoreceiver', PWR LED, Optical Input, 'Bias Monitor 1mV/uA', Made in USA. Powered from the New Focus 0901 supply (INS-003).
Wavelength Range: 800-865 nm - a NARROW NIR WINDOW, limited by the input lens dispersion, not by the detector material. THIS COVERS YOUR 810 nm SPDC LINE (FBP-009, HQ810/20) AND ESSENTIALLY NOTHING ELSE YOU OWN. It does NOT reach 1064 nm and it does NOT reach 1550 nm.
Aperture / Size: Optical input is FC/PC on 50 um core GRADED-INDEX MULTIMODE fibre - that is what the '-50' means (50 um core), NOT 50 ohms. The single-mode sibling is the 1474-A on 9 um fibre. Output is an Anritsu K connector, 50 ohms.

Notes (Function & Operating Range): IMPORTANT CORRECTION - THIS IS NOT A SINGLE-PHOTON DETECTOR. You recorded it as one, and it is worth being precise because the difference is about eight orders of magnitude in sensitivity. This is a LINEAR analog photoreceiver: a PIN photodiode with no internal gain, giving a continuous voltage proportional to instantaneous optical power, read on a scope or spectrum analyser. There is no discriminator, no TTL click output and no Geiger-mode bias. A REAL SINGLE-PHOTON DETECTOR (a Si SPAD like the Excelitas SPCM-AQRH, an InGaAs SPAD like the ID Quantique id230, or an SNSPD) has internal gain of 10^6 or more, so one absorbed photon makes a macroscopic digital pulse. You measure a COUNT RATE and the noise figure is dark counts per second, not NEP. WHY A PIN DIODE PHYSICALLY CANNOT DO IT: one 1550 nm photon liberates one electron, 1.6e-19 C. Even dumped into 50 ohms in 1 ns that is about 8 nV. Johnson noise in 50 ohms over 1 GHz is about 29 uV rms - the single-photon signal sits three to four orders of magnitude UNDER the thermal noise floor. You need roughly 10^3 to 10^5 simultaneous photons before a PIN diode produces anything above noise. FOR SCALE: 1 nW at 1550 nm is about 8 BILLION photons per second. A nanowatt is an enormous amount of light in photon-counting terms. WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY EXCELLENT AT: measuring the TIME STRUCTURE of a bright optical signal. At 22 GHz it resolves features down to about 15 ps, which is fast enough to see the individual 6 ps pulses from your supercontinuum (LSR-005) if you can get them into the 800-865 nm window. THE PRICE OF THAT SPEED IS SENSITIVITY: noise scales as the square root of bandwidth, so a 22 GHz receiver has a noise floor in the MICROWATT range. Compare DET-003 (Thorlabs DET110) at about 50 nW over 17.5 MHz. Fast and sensitive are opposites; pick one. MULTIMODE INPUT IS A REAL CONSTRAINT: 50 um graded-index fibre is telecom-datacom fibre, not the single-mode fibre your 1550 nm bench uses. You cannot simply plug an SMF-28 patch cord into it and expect the specified performance. IT NEEDS THE 0901 SUPPLY (INS-003) - it will not run on a battery like DET-002 or DET-003. WHICH DETECTOR DO I USE? THE SPEED LADDER IN THIS LAB, fastest first: DET-002 (New Focus 1011, 40 GHz) and DET-001 (New Focus 1484-A-50, 22 GHz) are THE HIGH-SPEED PAIR - these are the only detectors here fast enough for OPTICAL COMMUNICATIONS work: modulated data streams, eye diagrams, RF beat notes, heterodyne detection, and resolving the mode spacing of the femtosecond lasers. Everything else in the catalogue is orders of magnitude slower. DET-003 (Thorlabs DET110, Si) is a general-purpose biased photodiode - nanosecond class, fine for alignment, pulse detection and slow signals, useless above a few tens of MHz. The power-meter heads (MTR-002, MTR-006, MTR-007) are AVERAGE POWER sensors, not signal detectors - the thermopile MTR-007 has a thermal time constant of seconds. DET-004 and DET-005 (MPD SPADs) are the opposite extreme: single-photon sensitive but photon-COUNTING, giving TTL clicks with dead time, not a linear waveform. THE READOUT IS USUALLY WHAT LIMITS YOU, NOT THE DETECTOR: the only oscilloscopes in this catalogue are two LeCroy WaveAce 102 at 60 MHz (ELE-010). They cannot show anything these two fast detectors can resolve. To actually use 22 or 40 GHz of bandwidth you need a sampling scope, a real-time scope of comparable bandwidth, or an RF spectrum analyser - and matched 50 ohm coax with proper connectors throughout, since at these frequencies cable and connector quality dominates. ALSO NOTE THE BAND MISMATCH: DET-001 only covers 800-865 nm, so despite being the "comms-speed" pair it is DET-002 (if it is indeed InGaAs) that would reach the 1550 nm telecom bench. Confirm DET-002 detector material before planning a 1550 nm high-speed measurement around it. POWER: needs the current-limited New Focus 0901 supply (INS-003) - see that entry, it exists specifically to stop a wiring fault destroying this receiver front end.

Part Number: Round silver housing marked 'THORLABS DET110', CE. ON/OFF switch, BAT compartment, BNC output. DISCONTINUED - Thorlabs' current equivalent line is the DET-A2 series, and the DET36A2 matches this one's 13 mm2 active area and speed most closely.

Focal Length / Key Spec: Rise time 20 ns; catalogue bandwidth 17.5 MHz. NEP 1.2e-14 W/sqrt(Hz). Dark current 10 nA. Junction capacitance 20 pF. Damage threshold 100 mW CW; linearity limit about 1 mW.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): IMPORTANT CORRECTION - THIS IS NOT A SINGLE-PHOTON DETECTOR. You recorded it as one, and it is worth being precise because the difference is about eight orders of magnitude in sensitivity. This is a LINEAR analog photoreceiver: a PIN photodiode with no internal gain, giving a continuous voltage proportional to instantaneous optical power, read on a scope or spectrum analyser. There is no discriminator, no TTL click output and no Geiger-mode bias. A REAL SINGLE-PHOTON DETECTOR (a Si SPAD like the Excelitas SPCM-AQRH, an InGaAs SPAD like the ID Quantique id230, or an SNSPD) has internal gain of 10^6 or more, so one absorbed photon makes a macroscopic digital pulse. You measure a COUNT RATE and the noise figure is dark counts per second, not NEP. WHY A PIN DIODE PHYSICALLY CANNOT DO IT: one 1550 nm photon liberates one electron, 1.6e-19 C. Even dumped into 50 ohms in 1 ns that is about 8 nV. Johnson noise in 50 ohms over 1 GHz is about 29 uV rms - the single-photon signal sits three to four orders of magnitude UNDER the thermal noise floor. You need roughly 10^3 to 10^5 simultaneous photons before a PIN diode produces anything above noise. FOR SCALE: 1 nW at 1550 nm is about 8 BILLION photons per second. A nanowatt is an enormous amount of light in photon-counting terms. THE TERMINATION YOU CHOOSE CHANGES THIS DETECTOR BY A FACTOR OF TWENTY THOUSAND, and it is the single most misunderstood thing about it. Output voltage is V = I_photo x R_load, while bandwidth is 1/(2*pi*R_load*C_j) with C_j = 20 pF. Gain and bandwidth trade exactly inversely. INTO 50 OHMS: the RC limit is about 159 MHz, so the diode's own 20 ns rise time dominates and you get the catalogue 17.5 MHz - but the signal is tiny (microamps times 50 ohms is microvolts). Use this for pulses, modulation and nanosecond timing. INTO 1 MEGOHM (a scope's high-Z input): bandwidth collapses to roughly 8 kHz, but the signal is 20,000 times larger. Use this ONLY for DC or slow measurements. THE TRAP: people plug it into a high-Z scope input, see a beautiful large signal, and conclude the detector is slow or the laser is not pulsing. Terminate at 50 ohms and keep the cable short for anything fast; if the signal is then too small, add an amplifier rather than raising the load. WHY THE BATTERY: the A23 cell provides REVERSE BIAS. Without it the diode runs photovoltaic - much higher junction capacitance, far slower, and poor linearity. As the battery drains, capacitance rises and you lose bandwidth silently. Check it when results stop making sense. THIS IS THE RIGHT DETECTOR FOR MOST OF YOUR VISIBLE WORK - large area, forgiving alignment, 350-1100 nm, and a simple BNC out.

Notes (Function & Operating Range): REFLECTIVE AND ABSORPTIVE ND ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE, and choosing wrong causes two very specific problems. FIRST, A REFLECTIVE ND SENDS YOUR REJECTED LIGHT SOMEWHERE. It does not absorb the beam, it bounces it - so an ND 3 at normal incidence throws 99.9% of a 4 W supercontinuum straight back up the beam path toward the source. Tilt reflective NDs a few degrees and dump the reflection deliberately, or you get ghost beams, etalon fringes between the ND and the next surface, and in the worst case feedback into a laser. SECOND, THAT IS ALSO WHY THEY SURVIVE HIGH POWER. Because they reflect rather than absorb, they do not heat up and crack the way absorptive glass does. For LSR-005 (4 W) or LSR-001 (200 mW) a reflective ND is the correct choice and an absorptive one is a thermal-shock risk. COMPARE WITH FND-001 and FND-002 in this catalogue, which are ABSORPTIVE - those are the ones to use where a stray reflection matters more than heat. I have recorded them the other way round, because these three are metallic mirror-finish plates and the larger stack is varied grey and clear glass. If I have that backwards, say so and I will swap the two rows - but check a plate against a lamp first: a reflective ND looks like a dim mirror from the front, an absorptive one looks like grey glass. 'CAL-DET' most likely means this specific plate is the calibrated one used in front of a detector - if so it is the one whose OD somebody actually measured, and it should not be mixed in with the others.

Notes (Function & Operating Range): THESE TWO ARE THE BUTTERFLY-LASER CONTROLLER PAIR, but you cannot connect them to a 14-pin butterfly package directly. A butterfly diode brings the laser, its monitor photodiode, a TEC and a thermistor out on ONE 14-pin package, and a BUTTERFLY MOUNT is what breaks those into separate connectors: laser plus monitor PD to the driver, TEC plus thermistor to the temperature controller. NO BUTTERFLY MOUNT IS ANYWHERE IN THIS CATALOGUE. Without one these two are just a driver and a TEC controller with nothing to plug into. It is also what protects the diode: run a butterfly package hard with the TEC off and you cook it. THE THREE MODES ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE. Constant-T is what you want in normal operation. Notes (Function & Operating Range): GREEN MEANS APC. That colour convention is an industry standard, not a habit: green boot or body = APC (8 degree angled endface), blue = UPC single mode, beige or black = multimode or older PC. It is the fastest way to avoid mismating, and it is worth trusting. THE RETURN LOSS ON THE LABEL IS BAD FOR AN APC. Typical targets are about 40 dB for PC, 50 dB for UPC and 60 dB for APC. 36.1 dB is worse than a plain PC spec and roughly 24 dB - a factor of 250 in reflected power - short of what an 8 degree endface should deliver. TWO EXPLANATIONS, and it matters which: either the number on a cheap consumer label is generic boilerplate rather than a measurement of this cable, or the connector really is poorly polished or contaminated. MEASURE IT if back-reflection matters to you - and it does, because reflection into a laser diode causes mode hopping, RIN and linewidth broadening. That is the whole reason APC exists and the whole reason you have a 1550 nm narrow-linewidth source. NEVER MATE APC TO PC OR UPC. Two things go wrong at once. PHYSICALLY, an angled ferrule cannot make full contact with a flat or domed one - they meet at an edge, the spring force concentrates on that edge, and you can permanently scratch or chip BOTH endfaces, including the one on an instrument bulkhead you cannot easily replace. OPTICALLY, refracting out of the 8 degree face bends the beam by about 3.7 degrees, which costs roughly 2 dB, plus the air gap adds a strongly reflective interface at about -14 dB - defeating the entire point of APC. GREEN MATES ONLY TO GREEN. Your ACC-002 (SM1FCA2) is APC, so this is the cable that goes with it - not ACC-012.

Item Name: Fibre-optic tap coupler, 1x2, 980 nm, 1/99 split - WITH FACTORY TEST DATA
Manufacturer: E-TEK Dynamics, Inc., San Jose CA (acquired by JDS Uniphase in 2000)
Part Number: Case label and test sheet: 'Model No. SMFC7101PSA10 / Serial No. 700929554 / S/O: ITM-113 (Internal-R&D) / E-TEK Dynamics, Inc. / Made in U.S.A.' Tested 6/14/99, PASS INSPECTION stamp. Model number decode NOT CONFIRMED - E-TEK's ordering scheme is not published anywhere. 'SMFC' as Single Mode Fused Coupler is plausible (other vendors use it that way) but the digits cannot be decoded from any source.
Wavelength Range: 980 nm - one of the two standard erbium pump bands (the other is 1480 nm). NOT a signal-band device.
Aperture / Size: 1x2 fused coupler, 1.0 m leads, 250 um fibre package. Fibre is CORNING FLEXCORE 1060 (also sold as HI 1060): mode field diameter 5.9 um at 980 nm, cutoff 920 +/- 50 nm, NA 0.14, 125 um cladding, 245 um coating. Ports colour-coded: I1 and O1 clear, O2 red.
Focal Length / Key Spec: SPLIT RATIO 1/99. MEASURED ON THIS UNIT: I1 to O1 insertion loss 0.09 dB; I1 to O2 insertion loss 20.22 dB; PDL 0.05 dB. Grade P.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE ONLY OPTIC IN THIS ENTIRE CATALOGUE THAT ARRIVED WITH ITS OWN MEASURED TEST DATA. Keep the sheet with the part - it is worth more than the coupler. WHAT A 1/99 TAP AT 980 nm IS FOR: it is an EDFA PUMP MONITOR TAP. 980 nm pumps an erbium-doped fibre amplifier; you need to know the pump diode is actually lasing and at what power, for the control loop and for safety interlocks - but every milliwatt you divert is gain you lose. Tapping 1% costs only 0.044 dB of pump while still giving a photodiode an enormous signal: a 150 mW pump puts 1.5 mW on the tap. A 50:50 would throw away half the pump. THE NUMBERS ON THE SHEET ARE EXCELLENT AND SELF-CONSISTENT - I checked them. An ideal 1/99 gives 0.0436 dB on the through port and 20.00 dB on the tap. Working back from the measurements: O1 = 10^(-0.09/10) = 97.95%, O2 = 10^(-20.22/10) = 0.951%, summing to 98.905%. So EXCESS LOSS is only 0.048 dB - under 1.1% lost to scatter - which is very good for a fused biconic taper. Renormalised, the true split is about 0.96 : 99.04, right on spec. WHY IT MATTERS TO YOU SPECIFICALLY: 980 nm is the pump band for an EDFA, and DET-002 (New Focus 1011) is engraved for 980 nm too. If there is an erbium amplifier anywhere in this lab's history, this coupler and that detector are both parts of it. Worth asking whether an EDFA exists - it would transform what the 1550 nm bench can do. IT IS NOT A SIGNAL-BAND PART. At 1550 nm this coupler's split ratio and loss are unspecified and the fibre is past its design band. Do not press it into service as a 1550 nm tap. PROVENANCE: E-TEK was an independent San Jose passive-component maker, IPO'd December 1998, and JDS Uniphase announced its acquisition in January 2000 for about $15 billion in stock. This sheet is dated June 1999 - seven months before that announcement - so it is a genuine independent-E-TEK, US-made part.

Item Name: Fibre-optic beamsplitter - 1x2 WIDEBAND single-mode coupler, 1550 nm, 50:50
Part Number: Laser-marked on the red tube: 'THORLABS TW1550R5F1'. Hand-typed box label: '1x2 single-mode 1450-1650 nm 50:50 thorlabs TW1550R5F1'. Full Thorlabs product name for this family: '1x2 Wideband Fiber Optic Coupler, 1550 +/- 100 nm, 50:50 Split, FC/PC'. Still in its original Thorlabs carton with the fibre coiled on the card inserts.
Wavelength Range: 1450-1650 nm (1550 +/- 100 nm). THE 'W' IN THE PART NUMBER MEANS WIDEBAND - Thorlabs' narrowband sibling is the TN1550 series at 1550 +/- 15 nm, a band seven times narrower. You have the wide one, which is the more useful of the two for anything that is not a single fixed line.
Aperture / Size: 1x2: one common leg (white furcation, one FC connector) and two split legs (red furcation, two FC connectors). Single-mode fibre. YELLOW connector boots - see the notes, this is FC/PC, not APC.
Focal Length / Key Spec: 50:50 split across 1450-1650 nm. Exact insertion loss, excess loss, directivity and PDL for this specific SKU NOT CONFIRMED - Thorlabs' pages would not render for me. Expect roughly 3.2-3.6 dB per output for a good single-mode 50:50 (3.0 dB of that is the split itself) with excess loss under about 0.3 dB.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THIS IS THE ONE THAT WORKS ON YOUR 1550 nm BENCH - and that is the whole point of recording it separately from ACC-011. ACC-011 (TM105R5F1A) is the same idea in MULTIMODE at 400-900 nm; it is for the 810 nm SPDC side and it is useless at 1550. This one is SINGLE-MODE and centred on 1550. Between them you now have a 50:50 splitter for each of your two benches. SINGLE-MODE vs MULTIMODE IS NOT A DETAIL HERE. A single-mode coupler preserves the spatial mode, so the two outputs are mutually coherent and can be recombined - that is what makes an INTERFEROMETER possible. A multimode coupler scrambles the mode and cannot do that. So this part, and not ACC-011, is what you would build a Mach-Zehnder or a fibre interferometer from. WITH A SECOND ONE YOU HAVE A COMPLETE MACH-ZEHNDER: coupler one splits, two fibre arms, coupler two recombines. You own exactly one, so if that is the goal, order a second TW1550R5F1 - and buy the same part number, because matched couplers keep the interferometer balanced. CONNECTOR POLARITY - CHECK THIS BEFORE PLUGGING ANYTHING IN. The yellow boots and the 'F1' suffix both say FC/PC (flat polish). That means it mates with ACC-012 (the FiberStore FC/UPC patch cable) and it does NOT mate with ACC-002 (SM1FCA2, which is FC/APC) or with ACC-013 (the green-booted FC/APC cord). Thorlabs sells the APC version as TW1550R5A1 if you need it. WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN USUAL ON THIS BENCH: LSR-002 is a narrow-linewidth C-band source, and back-reflection into it causes mode hopping and linewidth broadening. An FC/PC interface reflects at roughly -40 dB against about -60 dB for APC. If you see the PPCL500 misbehaving after inserting this coupler, that is the first thing to suspect. PART NUMBER DECODED: T = coupler, W = WIDEBAND single-mode (N = narrowband, M = multimode), 1550 = centre wavelength, R5 = 50:50 ratio (R1 = 99:1, R2 = 90:10, R3 = 75:25), F1 = FC/PC-terminated 1x2 (A1 = FC/APC 1x2, F2 = FC/PC 2x2). IT IS STILL IN THE FACTORY CARTON WITH THE FIBRE PROPERLY COILED. Keep it that way when it is not in use - the card inserts hold the bend radius, and a single-mode fibre kinked below about 30 mm radius loses light at 1550 nm faster than at any shorter wavelength.

Item Name: POLARIZATION-MAINTAINING fibre coupler, 2x2, 1310 nm, 50:50 - WITH FACTORY TEST REPORT
Part Number: Test report: 'Polarization Maintaining Fiber Coupler Optical Test Report', dated Aug.03.2013, S/N L130250278, P/N PC1310-50-APC-1, description '1310 PMC 50/50', tested by Ying Liu, PASSED. PART NUMBER DECODED: PC = Thorlabs' 2x2 PM fused coupler prefix (PMC is the 1x2 family); 1310 = centre wavelength, +/-15 nm bandwidth; 50 = 50:50 split; APC = FC/APC connectors; trailing -1 = 1 m pigtails. STILL A CURRENT THORLABS PRODUCT.
Wavelength Range: 1310 +/- 15 nm - NARROWBAND, and NOT your 1550 nm band. This is the O-band, not the C-band.
Aperture / Size: 2x2: four FC/APC legs. Input 1 = BLACK lead, Input 2 = BLUE lead, Out 1, Out 2 = blue. Package Ø3.0 +/- 0.1 mm x 70 +/- 0.5 mm steel splice-protection tube. Fibre is Fujikura SM13-PR-U25A-H PANDA PM: MFD 9.0 um at 1310 nm, beat length 3.8-5.6 mm, cutoff 1.13-1.27 um, 125 um cladding, 245 um coating, 2% proof test.
Focal Length / Key Spec: MEASURED ON THIS UNIT - I1->O1: 51.0%, IL 3.35 dB, PER 26.18 dB. I1->O2: 49.0%, 3.53 dB, 21.50 dB. I2->O1: 49.9%, 3.80 dB, 20.41 dB. I2->O2: 50.1%, 3.79 dB, 18.55 dB. Directivity >=55 dB. Catalogue spec is >=18 dB PER.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE SECOND ITEM IN THIS CATALOGUE WITH ITS OWN MEASURED TEST DATA (after ACC-015). Keep the sheet with the part. WHAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM YOUR OTHER COUPLERS: it is POLARIZATION-MAINTAINING. ACC-011 and ACC-016 scramble polarisation; this one preserves it along a defined birefringent axis. That matters for anything where the polarisation state carries information - polarisation-encoded qubits, PM interferometry, or feeding a polarisation-sensitive modulator. PER IS THE SPEC THAT DEFINES A PM COUPLER. Launch light on one axis, measure the aligned and crossed power at the output; PER = 10log10(aligned/crossed). 20 dB means 1% of your power has leaked into the wrong polarisation. I READ THE FOUR NUMBERS AND THEY TELL A STORY: Input 1 gives 26.2 and 21.5 dB; Input 2 gives 20.4 and 18.6 dB. Input 2 drags BOTH of its outputs down, which points at Input 2's launch splice or connector being the weakest joint in the device. THE INSERTION LOSSES SAY THE SAME THING. Against the ideal for each measured split, the excess loss is 0.43 dB from Input 1 and 0.78 dB from Input 2 - I checked it by summing the output powers, and both sums are self-consistent. Same weak port. SO: USE INPUT 1. It is measurably the better side on both PER and loss, and there is no reason to leave that on the table. IS 18-20 dB GOOD? It is ordinary commercial grade and it is at the spec floor - Thorlabs quotes >=18 dB for this part. A good PM patch cable does 25-30 dB. If you need better, the current PN1310R5A2 is specified >=20 dB. THE REAL CATCH: THIS IS A 1310 nm PART AND YOUR BENCH IS 1550 nm. At 1550 the split ratio, loss and PER are all unspecified and the +/-15 nm bandwidth is long gone. Do not press it into service on the C-band. The direct sibling you would want is the PC1550-50-APC. IT IS FC/APC, so it mates with ACC-002 (SM1FCA2) and ACC-013 - and NOT with ACC-012, ACC-016 or ACC-021, which are all FC/PC.

Item Name: Pigtailed aspheric fibre collimator, EFL 2 mm, 1550 nm, FC/APC
Part Number: Tray label: 'CFS2-1550-APC', TP00344179, packed by Lourdes Beatriz. Thorlabs lists the exact EFL as 2.03 mm. Yellow single-mode pigtail, still coiled in the factory clamshell.
Wavelength Range: 1550 nm coating. Single-mode fibre pigtail.
Aperture / Size: EFL 2.03 mm. Small threaded barrel, factory-fixed focus. Exact housing dimensions and thread NOT CONFIRMED - Thorlabs' spec pages would not load for me.
Focal Length / Key Spec: OUTPUT BEAM, CALCULATED from SMF-28 at 1550 nm (MFD 10.4 um, w0 = 5.2 um): 1/e2 diameter D = 4*f*lambda/(pi*MFD) = 0.39 mm. Full-angle divergence 2*theta = 4*lambda/(pi*D) = 5.1 mrad, about 0.29 degrees. Rayleigh range about 75 mm.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): Thorlabs CFS series - PIGTAILED ASPHERIC COLLIMATORS, single-mode fibre (NOT PM). The number in the part name is the nominal focal length in mm; -APC means the pigtail is FC/APC terminated. A collimator this simple has one job: turn the diverging cone out of a fibre into a defined free-space beam, with the focus set at the factory so you cannot lose it. THE SHORT ONE - AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE CHOICE, NOT A LESSER VERSION. A 0.39 mm beam is small enough to pass through tight apertures, small optics and narrow-bore hardware, which is exactly what you want for compact fibre-to-fibre links or launching into a small modulator. BUT IT IS ONLY 'COLLIMATED' OVER A FEW CENTIMETRES. Rayleigh range about 75 mm means the beam has visibly grown by the time it has crossed 15 cm of table. If you need to send light any real distance, use ACC-019 instead. That is the whole difference between the two. COUNT NOT VERIFIED - the clamshell has two wells and I can see fibre in both, but only one connector clearly. Count them when you open it. IT IS FC/APC, which is the right polarity for ACC-002 and ACC-013 and the wrong one for your FC/PC parts.

Part Number: Tray label: 'CFS18-1550-APC / Pigtailed Aspheric Collimators, EFL 18mm, 1550nm', TP00912294, 'INSP 1256 1378 1602 1616'. Thorlabs lists the exact EFL as 18.75 mm.

Notes (Function & Operating Range): Thorlabs CFS series - PIGTAILED ASPHERIC COLLIMATORS, single-mode fibre (NOT PM). The number in the part name is the nominal focal length in mm; -APC means the pigtail is FC/APC terminated. A collimator this simple has one job: turn the diverging cone out of a fibre into a defined free-space beam, with the focus set at the factory so you cannot lose it. THE LONG-RANGE ONE, AND THE MORE USEFUL OF THE PAIR FOR MOST BENCH WORK. A 3.6 mm beam with 0.55 mrad divergence stays collimated across an entire optical table - the Rayleigh range is 6.4 m against 75 mm for ACC-018. COUNT: THE PACKING LABEL LISTS FOUR INSPECTION NUMBERS - 1256, 1378, 1602, 1616 - which normally means FOUR UNITS were packed and inspected. The tray shows two wells. COUNT THEM; if there really are four, this is the most numerous single optical component in the catalogue after the mirrors. Recorded as 4 pending a physical count. FOUR MATCHED COLLIMATORS WOULD BE WORTH KNOWING ABOUT - that is enough to build a full free-space link with a fibre in and a fibre out at both ends of an experiment, or a fibre Mach-Zehnder with free-space arms.

Item Name: TAPERED LENSED FIBRE, 630 nm, PM, 1.2 um spot
Part Number: Label: 'NANONICS / For 630 nm PM / Tapered Lensed Fiber with FC/PC/PM connector / Working distance 6 +/- 1 um / Spot diameter 1.2 +/- 0.2 um'. In a hinged clear case with the fibre coiled and the connector foam-blocked.
Wavelength Range: 630 nm, POLARIZATION MAINTAINING. FC/PC/PM connector - a keyed PM connector, so the fibre axis is defined relative to the key.
Aperture / Size: Working distance 6 +/- 1 um. Spot diameter 1.2 +/- 0.2 um. The fibre END IS THE LENS - the tip is drawn to a taper and rounded into a microlens; there is no separate optic.
Focal Length / Key Spec: EFFECTIVE NA, CALCULATED from the Gaussian output (w0 = 0.6 um, lambda = 0.63 um): theta = lambda/(pi*w0) = 0.334 rad = 19.1 deg, so NA is about 0.33 - roughly three times the NA of the bare fibre. RAYLEIGH RANGE z = pi*w0^2/lambda = 1.8 um, so the usable depth of focus is only about 3.6 um.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE MOST DELICATE OPTIC IN THIS ENTIRE CATALOGUE, and the numbers on the label are the reason. A 6 MICRON WORKING DISTANCE IS SMALLER THAN A RED BLOOD CELL. The tip must sit 6 um from the target, aligned to well under a micron laterally, with only +/-1.8 um of axial latitude before the spot blows up. That is not a manual-stage job - it needs a three-axis nanopositioner and live power feedback. AND THERE IS NO CRASH MARGIN. A stage slip, a vibration, or a sample that is not flat drives a drawn glass point into the surface. The taper has no protective coating and is mechanically weak in bending. Keep the tip guarded whenever it is not in use, and never move an axis toward the sample without watching. WHAT IT IS FOR: edge-coupling into a photonic waveguide (a 1.2 um spot matches a SiN or Si waveguide mode or an inverse-taper spot-size converter), coupling to a laser-diode facet, near-field and NSOM-adjacent work, microresonator and single-emitter excitation. Nanonics' core business is NSOM and multiprobe SPM, which is where this came from. 630 nm IS THE ODD PART FOR YOUR LAB. It is not 810 and it is not 1550 - it is HeNe territory, and LSR-004 is your 632.8 nm HeNe. If this fibre was bought for a visible-band photonics or NSOM experiment, that laser is its natural source. Ask what it was for; a lensed fibre is a specific tool bought for a specific job. IT IS PM, so the polarisation axis is fixed relative to the connector key - which is what you want for anything polarisation-sensitive and what makes it non-trivial to substitute with an ordinary lensed fibre. COMPARE WITH A GRIN-LENSED FIBRE, which gives millimetre working distances and loose alignment tolerance at the cost of a much larger spot. If your application does not strictly need 1.2 um, a GRIN version would be far easier to live with.
