Notes (Function & Operating Range): NOW FULLY IDENTIFIED from the rear nameplate - this was previously flagged as "model 130 vs 260 NOT CONFIRMED". It is a CS130B-3-MC, made October 2022, and it is the NEWER of the two monochromators here (INS-013 is the older 74000-series Cornerstone). MODEL STRING DECODED, and one part of it is commonly misread: "CS130B" = Cornerstone 130B, 1/8 m. "-3" = EXTENDED RANGE grating set - two ruled 600 g/mm gratings blazed at 400 nm and 1000 nm, giving 300-2200 nm. CONFIRMED against Newport configuration data. "-MC" = MICROMETER-DRIVEN CONTINUOUSLY ADJUSTABLE SLITS. It does NOT mean "motorised" - every CS130B is motorised in wavelength and grating selection regardless of suffix. The alternative suffix is -FH (fixed slit holders). WHY THE -3 CONFIGURATION MATTERS HERE: 300-2200 nm in one instrument spans essentially everything this lab works with - from the 405 nm violet line right through 800 nm Ti:Sapphire, 1064 nm and the whole 1550 nm telecom band. The other grating sets do not: -1 High Resolution is 280-1200 nm, -2 Holographic 280-1000 nm, -4 Near-IR 600-2200 nm. You have the broadest of the four. THE TRADE-OFF, so nobody is surprised: broad range is bought with LOW DISPERSION. At ~11 nm/mm, a 100 um slit gives about 1.1 nm of bandpass. That is fine for photoluminescence and lamp characterisation and far too coarse for laser linewidth work - use the HP 70951A OSA (MAJ-014) for anything narrow. CALIBRATION: the sticker reads calibrated 20 APR 24 but THE DUE DATE WAS NEVER FILLED IN. Treat the wavelength axis as approximately right and verify against a known line (a HeNe at 632.8 nm, LSR-004, is the easy in-house check) before trusting absolute numbers. One inconsistency worth knowing: Newport own web spec table lists 150 mm focal length on this product page while their datasheet and manual both say 130 mm. 130 mm is the credible figure.

Item Name: DICHROIC dual-band ultrafast mirror, 400 AND 800 nm, low GDD, 45 deg AOI, Ø25.4 mm
Part Number: Stock #24-322 (sold as #50055); label R5001047023-23135, Made in Lithuania
Wavelength Range: Dual band: 385-415 nm AND 770-830 nm
Aperture / Size: Ø25.4 mm x 6.35 mm +/-0.10, fused silica (Corning 7980)
Focal Length / Key Spec: Rs >99.9% at both bands; Rp >99.8% (395-415 nm) and >99.9% (770-820 nm); GDD <35 fs2 (400 nm band, s) and <20 fs2 (800 nm band, s)
Notes (Function & Operating Range): Filed under Dichroics at your instruction - the coating is wavelength-selective, reflecting two narrow bands and passing the rest. BUT READ THIS BEFORE USING IT, BECAUSE IT DOES NOT DO WHAT MOST DICHROICS DO: it reflects BOTH bands at once. Rs is >99.9% at 385-415 nm AND >99.9% at 770-830 nm. It STEERS the 800 nm fundamental together with its 400 nm second harmonic on a single optic - it does NOT split them apart. If you want to SEPARATE 400 from 800, that is a different part: FDM-002 (the Ti:Sapphire harmonic isolator) or FDM-004 (the CVI 90:10 at 800 nm). Between the two reflection bands - roughly 450-750 nm - this mirror transmits, which is the sense in which it is dichroic, but that region is not where you would use it. WHY IT EXISTS: in an SHG setup the fundamental and the harmonic have to travel the same path after the crystal. An ordinary broadband mirror either will not reflect both efficiently or will add dispersion; this one does both at once with GDD under 35 fs2 at 400 nm and under 20 fs2 at 800 nm, so it does not stretch the pulses. IBS coating on fused silica with a stress-compensating back layer. DESIGNED FOR 45 DEGREES - do not use it at normal incidence, the bands shift.

Item Name: AUTOFOCUS microscope camera, C-mount, in aluminium flight case
Part Number: Model NOT READ - ToupTek autofocus C-mount cameras are the XFCAM / XFCAMTOP / X5FCAM families ("F" in the model name = autofocus)
Wavelength Range: Visible
Aperture / Size: Blue anodised aluminium body; C-mount thread with a RED anodised ring inside; CE / FC / WEEE marks on top, QC PASS on the front
Focal Length / Key Spec: For this class: Sony Starvis / Starvis 2 BSI CMOS, 1/2 to 1/1.8 inch, 2-8 MP; 1080p60 to 4K; typically HDMI + USB + Wi-Fi + SD, 12 V DC power
Notes (Function & Operating Range): AUTOFOCUS CAMERA - confirmed by the lab. HOW THE AUTOFOCUS ACTUALLY WORKS, because it is not what most people assume: on ToupTeks C-mount AF cameras the camera MOVES ITS OWN SENSOR along the optical axis over a few millimetres and maximises contrast in a selectable region. It does NOT drive the microscope focus stage and there is no lens motor. THREE CONSEQUENCES WORTH KNOWING: (1) Sensor-shift focusing slightly CHANGES THE MAGNIFICATION as it moves, so the image scale drifts with focus position. For any calibrated measurement, either recalibrate at the focus position you are using or switch to manual focus. (2) It only has a few mm of travel, so it corrects RESIDUAL focus error - you still have to get the microscope roughly parfocal first with the C-mount adapter collar. That is exactly why it is useful on a stereo zoom scope, where focus shifts as you zoom. (3) DO NOT BOLT AN INFINITY-CORRECTED OBJECTIVE STRAIGHT ONTO IT. An infinity objective forms no image without a tube lens - the AF will simply hunt forever. It needs a trinocular head or a tube lens in front of it. THE RED RING INSIDE THE C-MOUNT is almost certainly the 5 mm C-to-CS spacer that ToupTek ships with these (C flange 17.526 mm, CS 12.5 mm). If you unscrew it you shift the back focus by exactly 5 mm and lose focus and parfocality - so leave it in unless you know why you are removing it. FLAG: NOT CONFIRMED for this unit; if the ring rotates and moves the sensor it is a back-focus preset instead. SOFTWARE: these run standalone off HDMI with the built-in XCamView menu system driven by a USB mouse - no PC needed - as well as through ToupView or ToupLite on a PC. ToupTek publish an SDK for Windows/Linux/macOS plus DirectShow, TWAIN, LabVIEW and MATLAB drivers and their own Micro-Manager plugin. There is no official Python binding; the community `NMGRL/toupcam` ctypes wrapper works for standard USB models. FLAG: SDK control of the AUTOFOCUS specifically is NOT CONFIRMED - autofocus is normally driven from the on-screen menu. TO PIN DOWN THE MODEL: read the string on the base plate, and note which ports it has - a 12 V DC barrel jack plus HDMI and an SD slot indicates the XFCAM autofocus family; USB only would indicate a non-AF body. IN USE HERE: paired with the 0.7x-4.5x C-mount zoom lens and focus rack (LEN-121) to form the improvised inspection microscope. Kept in its own aluminium flight case.

Item Name: 1-METHYL-2-PYRROLIDONE (NMP), >99.0%
Part Number: M0418; CAS 872-50-4; Lot ZVWWM-VS
Wavelength Range: GHS Danger - H360D MAY DAMAGE THE UNBORN CHILD (Repr. 1B), H315, H319, H335, H336, H373
Aperture / Size: 500 mL amber glass

Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE MOST HAZARDOUS CHEMICAL IN THIS CATALOGUE - READ THIS BEFORE USING IT. REPRODUCTIVE TOXICANT: NMP carries the EU CLP harmonised classification Repr. 1B, H360D "may damage the unborn child", with a specific concentration limit of 0.3%. It is under REACH Annex XVII restriction 71, which since May 2020 requires compliance with a DNEL of 14.4 mg/m3 inhalation and 4.8 mg/kg bw/day dermal. The EU indicative OEL is 40 mg/m3 8-h TWA WITH A "SKIN" NOTATION - meaning DERMAL uptake dominates, so gloves matter more than the hood. Nitrile breaks through NMP quickly; use butyl or laminate gloves, or nitrile-over-butyl, and change them often. Treat a warm NMP bath as a documented reproductive-hazard operation. WHAT IT IS FOR HERE: the back-end polymer-removal solvent - dissolving the PPC (or PMMA/PC) carrier film off a completed 2D heterostructure after transfer, where acetone alone leaves residue (a warm soak, typically 60-80 C, tens of minutes to overnight); stripping resist and doing metal lift-off when making contacts; general residue removal before AFM or annealing. A liquid-free alternative exists if you prefer: anneal at 350 C in Ar/3% H2 for 1 h, above PPCs ~280 C decomposition point. WHY THE LABEL SAYS "Store under Ar. Light Sensitive. Hygroscopic": all stability, not fire. It is water-miscible and pulls water from air, and wet NMP slowly hydrolyses and loses stripping performance. It also autoxidises at the ring position next to the nitrogen - an O2-driven, light-accelerated reaction - which is exactly why fresh NMP is colourless and old bottles go yellow. Oxidised NMP leaves residue in strip baths. So: argon blanket, amber bottle in a dark cabinet, cool (TCI recommends below 15 C), and do not keep an opened bottle for years. IF IT HAS GONE YELLOW, REPLACE IT. Also note US EPA has been restricting NMP under TSCA section 6 - check current status before reordering.

HOW IT IS USED: dissolve ~15 wt% PPC in anisole, spin onto a PDMS block at ~1500 rpm for a ~5 um film. PDMS gives the compliant mechanics; PPC gives the TEMPERATURE-TUNABLE ADHESION that PDMS alone cannot. Pick up the top flake (usually hBN) at ~40 C, just above Tg - softened PPC wets the flake and PPC-hBN adhesion beats hBN-SiO2. That hBN then picks up each subsequent layer at 40-60 C, building the stack top-down. RELEASE at ~90 C: PPC adhesion to the stack collapses (the crossover is around 70 C) and the film delaminates from the PDMS, depositing stack + PPC onto the target. Then strip the PPC in warm NMP (CHM-002) or anneal it away. STAY BELOW ~200 C during assembly or the PPC starts depolymerising. WHY IT LIVES IN THE FRIDGE (+2 to +8 C): because Tg is near ROOM TEMPERATURE. Warm pellets cold-flow and sinter into one solid mass, and the polycarbonate backbone slowly backbites to cyclic propylene carbonate, dropping Mn and degrading film quality. Keep it cold and dry, and LET THE BOTTLE WARM TO ROOM TEMPERATURE BEFORE OPENING so condensation does not get in. FLAG: the cold-storage rationale is the established literature mechanism, not a statement Sigma publishes.

Wavelength Range: Not classified - no GHS hazard. DOT: none
Aperture / Size: 4 L poly bottle; EXPIRY 4/7/31
Focal Length / Key Spec: ASTM D1193 Type II limits: conductivity <=1.0 uS/cm (resistivity >=1.0 MOhm.cm at 25 C), TOC <=50 ug/L, sodium <=5 ug/L, chloride <=5 ug/L, total silica <=3 ug/L. Label also claims filtration through a 0.2 um filter
Notes (Function & Operating Range): General rinsing, solution make-up and glassware work. KNOW WHAT TYPE II ACTUALLY GUARANTEES - IT IS NOT MUCH. Type II is a DISTILLATION grade defined mainly by >=1 MOhm.cm; Type I is >=18 MOhm.cm and 5x tighter on Na and Cl. COUNTERINTUITIVE BUT REAL: Type III (>=4 MOhm.cm) actually has a HIGHER minimum resistivity than Type II - the ASTM types are not a clean purity ladder, so do not assume II beats III on ionic purity. NOT ADEQUATE FOR A FINAL WAFER OR 2D-SAMPLE RINSE. The semiconductor standard is ASTM D5127, which demands 18.2 MOhm.cm, TOC 1-2 ppb (vs 50 ppb allowed here), metals at ppb-to-ppt and specified particle counts. At 5 ppb Na/Cl with no particle spec, Type II water leaves ionic and particulate residue when it dries. Use it for pre-cleans and glassware; get Type I / UPW for anything that touches a finished flake. WHY BOTTLED WATER HAS AN EXPIRY (4/7/31, a 5-year shelf life): high-purity water has no buffering capacity, so it absorbs atmospheric CO2 into carbonic acid and the resistivity falls - exposed Type I water drops from 16 to about 1 MOhm.cm in 48 hours, and HDPE is gas-permeable so even a sealed bottle equilibrates slowly. TOC also creeps up from bottle leaching. So a five-year-old bottle is likely sitting AT the 1 MOhm.cm limit rather than comfortably above it. The date is a specification-conformance date, not a safety date. FLAG: two photos of this appear to be the SAME bottle (identical lot and expiry) - recorded as Qty 1; tell me if there are actually two. Also NOT CONFIRMED: the 0.2 um filtration claim is on the label but appears on no distributor listing, and it is a Type I requirement, not a Type II one - i.e. LabChem going beyond spec. (3) Make a SHORT NICK AT THE WAFER EDGE ONLY, about 1-3 mm, aligned to the flat - do NOT drag a scribe across the face. A shallow narrow nick beats a deep one: a heavy scribe seeds microcracks that steer the fracture off-plane and sheds particles across your device area. (4) Break with an even three-point load - cleaving pliers close to the edge, or lay the wafer over a thin rod placed under the scribe line and press evenly on both sides. The crack follows the plane by itself. (5) Halves to quarters, every scribe parallel or perpendicular to the flat. Keep the scribed face away from the device side. Thiol-ene is oxygen-inhibited at the free surface, so an under-dosed joint keeps a tacky skin, outgasses unreacted monomer, and drifts in index and dimension. Give it the full 2 J/cm2 measured at 365 nm, cure under a cover slip or nitrogen where you can, and POST-BAKE 12 h at 50 C - full adhesion only develops after that (or a week at room temperature). Bond at the edge or annulus, outside the clear aperture, and keep it out of high-intensity beams generally - Norland publishes no laser damage threshold. Per your note, roughly half are plain silicon (300 MICRONS thick) and half are double-side-polished silicon nitride with 300 NANOMETRES of LPCVD SiN. The two numbers are both "300" but differ by a factor of a thousand, which is exactly the kind of thing that goes wrong at 2 am. WHY LPCVD SPECIFICALLY MATTERS: LPCVD nitride is deposited at 700-800 C and is dense, pinhole-free, low in hydrogen and highly conformal - far better than PECVD nitride as an etch mask, a diffusion barrier, or a mechanical membrane layer. It is also under high tensile stress, which is why free-standing structures in it are usually made low-stress (compare WFR-014). Double side polished means you can work from either face and transmit light through it. The cassette is marked with your name - worth adding a proper printed label (TLS-024) so the mixed contents are obvious to anyone else who opens it.

Item Name: HARMONIC ISOLATOR / SEPARATOR for a Ti:SAPPHIRE laser - elliptical dichroic, ~45 deg AOI
Manufacturer: Not marked on the optic or the mount - almost certainly an OEM part from a Ti:Sapphire laser head (Coherent or Spectra-Physics class)
Part Number: No manufacturer part number. Printed label on the table reads "TiS harmonic isolator ubs21" - "ubs21" is an internal inventory tag, not a maker P/N
Wavelength Range: READ FROM THE COATING, NOT FROM A DATASHEET: it appears deep BLUE-VIOLET in reflection, so the coating is HIGH-REFLECTING in the blue/violet (around 400 nm) and TRANSMITTING in the yellow-red and near-infrared. Best reading: reflects the ~400 nm SECOND HARMONIC and passes the ~800 nm Ti:Sapphire FUNDAMENTAL. NOT CONFIRMED - measure it.
Aperture / Size: ELLIPTICAL clear aperture, roughly 33 x 23 mm (MEASURE). Held by a slotted retaining ring in a machined oval flange with three cap screws
Focal Length / Key Spec: The ELLIPSE IS THE SPECIFICATION: an aspect ratio near 1.41 (= 1/cos 45 deg) means the optic is cut so that a ROUND beam fills a round footprint when the optic sits at 45 DEGREES. Install it at any other angle and both the aperture and the coating design are wrong.
Notes (Function & Operating Range): WHAT IT DOES: a harmonic isolator (harmonic separator) sits in a Ti:Sapphire beam path and splits the fundamental from its second harmonic - passing one and dumping the other - so that blue/UV light generated by parasitic doubling, or residual pump light, does not travel where it should not. In this lab that means the Coherent Vitesse (LSR-008) and Chameleon (LSR-009), and the SHG setup they feed. NOTE IT PAIRS WITH MIR-012: the Edmund 24-322 dual-band mirror steers 400 AND 800 nm together with low GDD; THIS optic does the opposite job - it SEPARATES them. Between the two you can route a fundamental and its harmonic independently. HOW TO SETTLE THE SPECIFICATION IN FIVE MINUTES, since nothing is marked: put it in front of a white source and look at the TRANSMITTED colour - if it passes amber/red and blocks blue, the reading above is right. For a real number, run a white lamp through it into the Ocean Optics USB4000 (INS-016) or a Cornerstone monochromator (INS-013/014) AT 45 DEGREES, not at normal incidence - dichroic edges shift with angle, so a normal-incidence measurement will give you the wrong cut-on. PROVENANCE QUESTION WORTH ASKING: an OEM elliptical optic in a purpose-machined flange normally lives INSIDE a laser head. If it came out of one of the Ti:Sapphire lasers, that laser may be missing a part - worth confirming before someone spends a day debugging stray blue light on the Vitesse or Chameleon. HANDLING: the coating is exposed and the aperture is large; hold the flange only, blow dust off with the bulb blower (TLS-046), and store it face-protected. FLAG: manufacturer, part number, exact cut-on wavelength, reflection band, damage threshold and design AOI are ALL UNCONFIRMED. Everything above is read off the optic itself and the printed label.

Item Name: RULED DIFFRACTION GRATINGS, two off, 600 g/mm - INSTALLED INSIDE the CS130B-3-MC monochromator
Manufacturer: Newport / Oriel (supplied as the CS130B "-3" Extended Range grating set)
Part Number: Part of configuration CS130B-3-MC; individual grating part numbers not marked externally
Wavelength Range: Grating 1 blazed at 400 nm; Grating 2 blazed at 1000 nm. Together they give the instrument its 300-2200 nm range.
Aperture / Size: Two gratings on a motorised two-position turret, both installed and pre-aligned
Focal Length / Key Spec: 600 grooves/mm on BOTH gratings, so groove spacing d = 1667 nm. Reciprocal dispersion 11 nm/mm (G1) and 10.6 nm/mm (G2)
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THESE ARE NOT LOOSE OPTICS - they live inside INS-014 and are selected by motor, so they are catalogued here only so the instrument capability is searchable. Do not go looking for them in a drawer. WHY TWO GRATINGS WITH THE SAME LINE DENSITY: the groove density sets the DISPERSION and the blaze sets where the EFFICIENCY PEAKS. Both are 600 g/mm so both disperse the same, but G1 peaks in the near-UV/blue and G2 peaks in the near-infrared. You switch gratings not to change resolution but to stay near peak efficiency - using the 400 nm grating out at 1600 nm would work geometrically and throw away most of your light. RULE OF THUMB: a blazed grating is usefully efficient roughly from 2/3 to 2x its blaze wavelength. So G1 covers about 270-800 nm and G2 about 670-2000 nm, which is exactly how the 300-2200 nm system figure is built. Crossover is around 700-800 nm - if you scan across that region, check which grating is selected. WATCH FOR SECOND ORDER: at 600 g/mm, light at 800 nm appears in first order at the same angle as 400 nm in second order. When measuring above roughly 800 nm with a broadband source you need an order-sorting longpass filter in front of the entrance slit or you will record a phantom peak. This catalogue has suitable filters - FLP-016 (700 nm cut-on), FLP-017 (550 nm), FLP-011 (900 nm) and FLP-015 (1500 nm). SEPARATE FROM GRT-001, which is a loose Thorlabs GR25-0616 (600 g/mm, 1600 nm blaze) you can build with.

A plate beamsplitter at 45 degrees is almost never truly 50:50 for both polarisations unless it was designed to be. If your measurement depends on the split ratio, MEASURE IT for your actual polarisation with the 1830-R power meter (MTR-008) rather than trusting "50/50". (2) PLATE OR CUBE, AND WHICH FACE? If it is a plate, one face is the coating and the other is AR - orientation matters, and a plate in a converging beam adds astigmatism. There will also be a ghost reflection from the second surface. (3) DESIGN ANGLE is presumably 45 degrees but is not stated. FLAG: manufacturer, part number, substrate, split tolerance, polarisation dependence and damage threshold are all UNKNOWN. Worth measuring the split ratio once and writing it on the label.

Item Name: FIBRE CONNECTOR INSPECTION MICROSCOPE, handheld, with adapter set and soft case

Notes (Function & Operating Range): THIS FILLS A REAL GAP. Under TLS-049 I noted that the USB digital microscope is NOT usable as a fibre inspection scope - this is the proper tool. Given how much fibre is in this catalogue (roughly thirty patch cables, couplers and collimators), and that contamination is the single largest cause of insertion-loss and return-loss failures, this should be in routine use. THE WORKFLOW IS: INSPECT -> CLEAN (with the FCC-7020 cassette, TOO-004) -> RE-INSPECT -> CONNECT. Never mate a connector you have not looked at. A single 5 um particle sitting on a 9 um single-mode core is most of the light path, and mating a dirty connector transfers the dirt onto the good one and can pit both ferrules under optical power. WHAT TO LOOK FOR - the IEC 61300-3-35 zones, by diameter: A = core, 0-25 um; B = cladding, 25-115 um; C = adhesive, 115-135 um; D = contact, 135-250 um. For single-mode PC the rule of thumb is NOTHING at all in zone A - no scratches, no defects - and in zone B, defects under 2 um unlimited, 2-5 um at most five, nothing over 5 um. (Edition 3 of the standard dropped zones C and D from pass/fail and gives measured optical performance precedence over a failed visual.) READ THE WARNING LABEL SERIOUSLY - IT IS NOT BOILERPLATE. "Do not use this microscope to look at the active optical fiber." Three compounding reasons: (1) 1310 and 1550 nm are INVISIBLE, so there is no blink reflex and no aversion response - you get no warning at all that you are being exposed; (2) the powers on this bench are not small - the two EDFAs (MAJ-005, MAJ-010) run to hundreds of mW; (3) THE MICROSCOPE MAKES IT WORSE, NOT BETTER: a bare fibre end is largely self-limiting because the output diverges at NA ~0.14 and spreads within centimetres, but this objective COLLECTS THE WHOLE CONE and delivers it into your eye. The optic removes exactly the protection that divergence gives you. RULE: confirm the fibre is dark with a power meter (MTR-008) or a visual fault locator BEFORE putting a connector into this scope, and never inspect a port on a live system. A video probe puts a camera at the image plane instead of your retina and is the safer tool if you are ever unsure. FLAG: brand, magnification and the exact adapter complement are not recorded - check what is actually in the case.

Item Name: GLAN-LASER calcite polarizer, 10 mm aperture, in a Thorlabs rotation mount
Part Number: MGLB10  (from the printed label: "karl lambrechat GLAN laser MGLB10")
Wavelength Range: Visible to near-infrared, roughly 350 nm to 2.3 um (non-UV natural calcite)
Aperture / Size: 10 mm clear aperture (the "10" in the part number); mounted in a black anodised housing, seated in a Thorlabs 360 degree graduated rotation mount
Focal Length / Key Spec: Air-spaced two-prism calcite Glan-Laser. Extinction ratio 1e-4 (about 10,000:1) for B-grade. Transmission 86-88% uncoated above 500 nm. Beam deviation 3-5 arc min. NO ESCAPE WINDOW on this variant
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE HIGHEST-PERFORMANCE POLARIZER IN THE CATALOGUE, and the one to use where extinction actually matters. PART NUMBER DECODED: M = mounted, GL = Glan-Laser, B = calcite quality grade B (>1 wave wavefront deformation from striae; KLCC A grade is 1/4 to 1 wave, S and E are tighter), 10 = 10 mm clear aperture. AN IMPORTANT CAVEAT ABOUT THE NAME - DO NOT ASSUME "LASER" MEANS HIGH POWER. KLCC "MGLB" is the variant with NO ESCAPE WINDOW. In any Glan-type prism the rejected ordinary ray is totally internally reflected at the air gap; with no escape window it is absorbed inside the prism, in the blackened side wall, where it heats the calcite and the paint. The high-power members of the family are the MGLA-SW / MGLA-DW / MGLS-SW / MGLS-DW parts, which have one or two polished side windows to let that beam out - those are the ones rated to the ~500 W/cm2 CW / 500 MW/cm2 pulsed class. THIS ONE IS NOT. Treat it as a low-to-moderate-power part and keep it out of the Ti:Sapphire and amplified beams (LSR-008, LSR-009, MAJ-005, MAJ-010). HOW IT COMPARES WITH WHAT YOU ALREADY HAVE: POL-001/002 are Glan-Taylor GT5 (5 mm aperture) and POL-003 is a GT10 (10 mm, unmounted). Glan-Laser is geometrically the same air-spaced design as Glan-Taylor but built from laser-grade low-striae calcite with a better polish, so it scatters less and has a cleaner wavefront - which is why it is worth more than the GT10 despite the same aperture. All of these beat a cemented Glan-Thompson for power handling, because there is no optical cement to absorb. PRACTICAL: calcite is SOFT and CLEAVES - do not touch the faces, do not overtighten the mount, and do not drop it. The acceptance angle is only about 8-10 degrees in the visible and narrows badly in the infrared, so it needs a well-collimated beam. Already in a graduated rotation mount, so the angle is directly readable. FLAG: the specific damage threshold for the no-escape-window MGLB variant is not published - NOT CONFIRMED.

Item Name: WEDGE PRISMS, 0.5 degree beam deviation, VIS-NIR coated - TWO UNITS, sealed
Part Number: PN 49437 (stock #49-437); "PRISM WEDGE 0.5 DEG VIS-NIR TS"; PO P00000153683 0-241008; Made in Singapore
Wavelength Range: VIS-NIR AR coated, 400-1000 nm
Aperture / Size: O25.0 mm (+0.00 / -0.10), centre thickness 3.00 mm; N-BK7
Focal Length / Key Spec: BEAM DEVIATION 0.5 degrees at 633 nm (0.87 dioptres). NOTE the physical WEDGE ANGLE is 0 deg 58 min (about 0.967 deg) - Edmund names these parts by DEVIATION, not by apex angle. Surface quality 20-10 scratch-dig; flatness 0.50/0.20 fringes at 632.8 nm
Notes (Function & Operating Range): READ THE PART NAME CAREFULLY - "0.5 DEG" IS THE BEAM DEVIATION, NOT THE WEDGE ANGLE. The glass is actually wedged by about 0.967 degrees; the deviation follows from delta = (n-1) x alpha, and with N-BK7 at n = 1.5151 that gives 0.5151 x 0.967 = 0.498 degrees. Getting this backwards is a common and expensive mistake in a design. Because n is dispersive, the deviation drifts slightly with wavelength (about 0.499 deg at 588 nm, 0.491 deg at 1064 nm) - a wedge is mildly chromatic, which matters for broadband use. WHAT WEDGES ARE FOR HERE - three jobs: (1) FINE BEAM STEERING. One wedge tilts a beam 0.5 degrees. TWO counter-rotating wedges (a Risley pair) give continuously variable deviation from 0 to 1.0 degrees in ANY azimuth - which is exactly why there are two of these. That is a far finer and more stable adjustment than walking a kinematic mirror. (2) BEAM SAMPLING. The Fresnel reflection off a face gives a low-power monitor pick-off that is ANGULARLY SEPARATED from the ghost off the second face, so the two do not overlap. (3) KILLING ETALON FRINGES - and this is the one worth understanding. In a PLANE-PARALLEL plate the two surface reflections are collinear and recombine coherently, making a low-finesse Fabry-Perot whose transmission ripples with wavelength and with temperature. Those periodic fringes are what wreck absorption and cavity spectroscopy. A WEDGE makes the two reflections non-parallel, so the second-surface ghost simply walks out of the beam and never interferes. Same reason laser windows, etalon substrates and beam samplers are wedged. Both units still sealed in their Edmund bags. "TS" = TECHSPEC, Edmund in-house designed line. SECOND PHOTO, PROBABLY THE SAME PAIR: two unmounted ~25 mm discs on lens tissue, with a printed lab label reading "widge plate" (wedge plate). Same quantity, same size class. I have NOT created a second row for them, on the assumption these are the Edmund 49437 pair unpacked and labelled. IF THAT IS WRONG AND YOU HAVE A SECOND, SEPARATE PAIR OF WEDGES, TELL ME and I will add them - the count matters here, because two wedges is exactly a Risley pair and four would be two pairs.

Item Name: BBO nonlinear crystal in a rotation mount - STORED UNDER ARGON
Part Number: No part number - printed label reads "bbo in Ar"
Wavelength Range: Not marked. Beta-BBO transmits roughly 190 nm to 3.5 um; the phase-matching angle sets what it actually doubles - NOT MARKED here
Aperture / Size: Optic seated in an SM1-threaded bore in a Thorlabs 360 degree graduated rotation mount
Focal Length / Key Spec: Cut angle, thickness, phase-matching type and design wavelength are ALL UNMARKED
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE LABEL IS THE IMPORTANT PART: "in Ar" means it is stored under ARGON, and that is not fussiness. BETA-BBO IS HYGROSCOPIC - atmospheric moisture attacks the polished faces and produces a permanent hazy, etched surface that scatters and cannot be polished out in a normal lab. A degraded BBO face is a dead crystal. So: keep it sealed, keep it dry, and if it has been out in room air for a long period, inspect the faces under magnification before assuming it still works. Some groups keep BBO in a desiccator or under a slow argon purge for exactly this reason - the vacuum desiccator (MAJ-020) is available if you want a dry store. THE ROTATION MOUNT MATTERS TOO: BBO is birefringent and angle-phase-matched, so the conversion efficiency depends steeply on the crystal angle. Being in a graduated rotation mount means the phase-matching angle is settable and readable - but note a rotation mount rotates about the BEAM axis, which sets the polarisation orientation, while phase matching also needs TILT. Check what degree of freedom you actually have before assuming you can tune it. POSSIBLE DUPLICATE - CHECK BEFORE COUNTING IT TWICE. This catalogue already has NLC-002 ("BBO", gold-ring mounted on a 3D-printed holder) and NLC-003 (a fully specified beta-BBO SHG crystal, NLC07, 3.00 mm, theta = 19.8 deg, in a O1 inch housing). This one may be NLC-003 taken out of its box and put into a rotation mount. Compare the housing engraving - NLC-003 has everything engraved on it, so if this housing carries "NLC07" they are the same crystal and the rows should be merged. FLAG: if it is NOT NLC-003, then nothing about this crystal is specified and it cannot be designed with - only experimented with. Worth pulling it out and reading the housing.

Under CAM-001 (ASI178MM) I called that one "the one to use for photon-starved work" - that was true of the six cameras then recorded. This one is better for long exposures, and the reason is the cooling. WHY COOLING ACTUALLY MATTERS, and it is not a small effect: dark current roughly HALVES EVERY 6-7 C. Taking the sensor from +25 C ambient down to -15 C is about six halvings - roughly 1/64 of the thermal signal. The point is not the dark level itself (you subtract that) but the SHOT NOISE ON IT, which goes as the square root of the dark electrons and CANNOT be calibrated away. For a 300 s exposure that is the difference between being dark-noise-limited and being read-noise or signal limited. REGULATED set-point cooling has a second benefit: a dark library taken once at a fixed sensor temperature stays valid across sessions. An uncooled camera drifts with ambient and with self-heating, so its darks never quite match. AND IT IS MONO. No Bayer filter array, so every pixel sees every photon in the passband - roughly 2-3x the effective per-pixel QE of a colour sensor, full spatial resolution with no demosaic interpolation, and it lets you put a NARROW BANDPASS in front and integrate for hours on one line. Item Name: Ø1 inch N-BK7 lens, hand-marked "LB1596A f=2.5m" - THE MARKING IS SELF-CONTRADICTORY
Part Number: Hand-written on the edge: "LB1596A  f=2.5m"
Wavelength Range: If it is genuinely an LB1596-A: broadband AR coated 350-700 nm
Aperture / Size: Ø1 inch (25.4 mm), unmounted
Focal Length / Key Spec: THE TWO HALVES OF THE MARKING DISAGREE - see notes
Notes (Function & Operating Range): READ THIS BEFORE PUTTING IT IN A LAYOUT. Thorlabs LB1596-A is a Ø1 inch N-BK7 BI-CONVEX lens of f = 60.0 mm (R1 = +61.0, R2 = -61.0 mm, centre thickness 4.7 mm, edge 2.0 mm). It is NOT a 2.5 m lens. The Thorlabs Ø1 inch N-BK7 f = 2500 mm part is LA1259 (plano-convex). So either this is an LB1596-A that was mis-annotated with the wrong focal length, or it is an LA1259 that was written up under the wrong part number. THE TWO-SECOND TEST, and they are easy to tell apart: an f = 60 mm lens is OBVIOUSLY CURVED with a thin 2 mm edge and a fat middle; an f = 2.5 m lens looks essentially FLAT, with near-uniform thickness and a sagitta of a few microns - it is easy to mistake for a window. Better still, image a distant ceiling light onto a card: at 60 mm you will find the focus by hand in seconds; at 2.5 m you will not find it on the bench at all. IF IT TURNS OUT TO BE THE f = 2.5 m LENS, that is the more interesting outcome - a very weak positive element is what you use for MODE MATCHING TO A CAVITY (cavity waists are large and far away, so matching almost always needs one or two long-focal-length lenses), as the long element of a high-magnification beam expander, or to add a controlled small amount of wavefront curvature without changing beam size. The practical difficulty is that the focus is 2.5 m away, so characterising it needs a folded path or a long rail, and the depth of focus is metres so the waist POSITION is very poorly defined by inspection. FLAG: identify it physically and re-label it. Right now this row cannot be designed with.

Item Name: COMPRESSED-AIR FILTER / WATER SEPARATOR, 1/4 inch port
Part Number: AF2000-02; marked PRESS. 0.05~0.85 MPa; Made in China
Wavelength Range: n/a
Aperture / Size: Port "-02" = 1/4 inch, most likely BSPT (PT1/4) on a Chinese unit - CHECK BEFORE THREADING; transparent polycarbonate bowl with a sintered bronze element and a manual drain screw
Focal Length / Key Spec: Operating pressure 0.05-0.85 MPa (about 7-123 psi). Filtration rating NOT CONFIRMED for this clone - genuine SMC AF20 is 5 um, clones are commonly 25-40 um
Notes (Function & Operating Range): FIRST-STAGE AIR PREPARATION. It does two jobs at once: a swirl vane flings LIQUID WATER AND OIL AEROSOL out against the bowl wall, and the sintered bronze element traps PARTICULATE - pipe scale, rust, PTFE tape shreds, compressor debris. The drain screw at the bottom bleeds the collected condensate, and on a MANUAL drain like this someone actually has to open it periodically or the bowl fills and the separated water gets carried back into the outlet. WHERE IT GOES: always FIRST in the chain - filter, then regulator, then (only if a tool needs oil) lubricator. Filter first so the regulator seat never sees grit or slugs of water. DO NOT PUT A LUBRICATOR ANYWHERE UPSTREAM OF THE SPIN COATER OR ANYTHING OPTICAL - oil mist is precisely the contaminant you are trying to keep off samples. WHY THIS LAB NEEDS IT: the Laurell spin coater (MAJ-021) requires N2 or clean dry air at 60-70 psi for its SEAL PURGE, and Laurell manual is explicit that the gas must be MOISTURE FREE, recommending a point-of-use filter of 1 um or less after the regulator. That purge keeps solvent vapour and resist out of the motor bearing - it is what makes the machine last. It also matters for blow-off drying after acetone/IPA, where a single 5 um particle blown onto a 10 um flake ruins the sample. SAFETY - THE POLYCARBONATE BOWL IS THE REAL HAZARD HERE, AND IT IS A DOCUMENTED FAILURE MODE, NOT A THEORETICAL ONE. Polycarbonate suffers environmental stress cracking from acetone, MEK, toluene, chlorinated solvents, ammonia, methanol and some synthetic compressor oils. A cracked bowl at 8 bar does not fail gracefully - IT SHATTERS AND THROWS FRAGMENTS. Rules: clean it with soapy water ONLY, never solvent; do not mount it next to the solvent bench or a fume hood plenum; depressurise before opening the drain or unscrewing the bowl; keep it out of sunlight (PC yellows and embrittles); and replace it at any sign of crazing or cloudiness. In a lab that handles acetone and IPA daily, a METAL-BOWL variant is the correct choice. FLAG: micron rating and whether the 1/4 inch port is BSPT or NPT are both unconfirmed - BSPT and NPT will start to thread together and then leak or crack the boss.

Item Name: UNIDENTIFIED optic in a Thorlabs graduated rotation mount - PURPLE/VIOLET COATING
Manufacturer: Optic unmarked; mount is a Thorlabs graduated rotation mount with a vernier index at 0
Part Number: No part number on the optic or the mount
Wavelength Range: NOT MARKED. The coating reflects PURPLE/VIOLET, which in this catalogue has been a reliable tell for an AR coating optimised in the NEAR-INFRARED (see POL-007 and FDM-003) - a coating tuned for 1050-1700 nm is far off-band in the visible and reflects with the residual peaking toward the red/violet. So: probably an IR optic. NOT CONFIRMED.
Aperture / Size: Optic appears Ø1 inch class, seated deep in an SM1-threaded bore; 360 degree graduated dial with a separate vernier index plate at 0
Focal Length / Key Spec: UNDETERMINED
Notes (Function & Operating Range): RECORDED AS UNIDENTIFIED rather than guessed. WHAT THE PHOTO ACTUALLY SHOWS: an optic with a violet-reflecting coating, mounted in a graduated ROTATION mount fitted with a vernier index - and that last detail is the most informative thing here. YOU DO NOT PUT AN OPTIC IN A GRADUATED ROTATION MOUNT UNLESS ITS ORIENTATION ABOUT THE BEAM AXIS MATTERS. That rules out plain lenses, windows, mirrors and most filters, and points at a POLARIZER or a WAVEPLATE. The vernier suggests someone cared about setting the angle to better than a degree, which leans toward a waveplate (where you set a specific angle relative to the fast axis) rather than a polarizer used as a simple on/off. HOW TO SETTLE IT IN TWO MINUTES: put it between two crossed polarizers (POL-001/002 are Glan-Taylors) and rotate it. A POLARIZER will null completely twice per revolution. A HALF-WAVE PLATE will pass light with four nulls per revolution as it rotates the polarisation. A QUARTER-WAVE PLATE will never fully null once you are off the axes. A plain window or filter will do nothing at all. Then check transmission at 633 nm versus 1550 nm to pin the band. Once identified, this row should be re-filed under Polarizers or Waveplates and given a proper label with the printer (TLS-024).

Item Name: ULTRAFAST BEAMSPLITTER, 800 nm, 90% reflectance, 45 deg, P-POLARIZATION - UNOPENED
Manufacturer: CVI Melles Griot (now CVI Laser Optics / IDEX)
Wavelength Range: 800 nm design wavelength. An 800 nm ultrafast design of this class is typically usable across roughly 730-870 nm - NOT CONFIRMED for this exact part.
Aperture / Size: Still sealed in its CVI clamshell - dimensions not recorded. CVI ultrafast beamsplitter plates are typically thin (1.0-1.75 mm) and WEDGED, in 1/2, 1 or 2 inch diameters
Focal Length / Key Spec: 90% reflectance at 45 degrees for P-POLARIZATION (so nominally a 90:10 split). Ultrafast dielectric coating on UV-grade fused silica, designed for near-zero group delay dispersion
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE PUMP-PROBE SPLITTER FOR THE Ti:SAPPHIRE BENCH. A 90:10 at 800 nm is the classic pump-probe element - 90% into the pump arm, 10% into the probe - or a 10% diagnostic tap to an autocorrelator (INS-015), spectrometer or power meter while 90% goes to the experiment. Pairs with the Vitesse (LSR-008) and Chameleon (LSR-009). THE "P" IS NOT DECORATION - READ IT BEFORE USING IT. At 45 degrees, p-polarization sits toward Brewster (56.6 deg for fused silica), so bare-surface p-reflectance is only about 0.6% versus about 9% for s. Every layer pair in the stack has weaker index contrast in p, which makes 90% R in p genuinely harder to achieve than in s. CONSEQUENCE: this coating is specified and guaranteed ONLY for p-polarised light at 45 degrees. Feed it s-polarised light and it will reflect FAR MORE than 90% and your split ratio is simply wrong. Check your polarisation before you trust the ratio. WHY GDD MATTERS HERE, and how much: a 100 fs pulse at 800 nm carries about 10 nm of bandwidth. Broadening goes as sqrt(1 + (4 ln2 x GDD / tau^2)^2), and with tau^2 = 1e4 fs^2 a few hundred fs^2 only stretches it a few percent - tolerable. At 20 fs (tau^2 = 400 fs^2) the same 300 fs^2 MORE THAN DOUBLES the pulse. So low-GDD matters mildly at 100 fs and is essential below about 30 fs. Also note the substrate itself: fused silica adds about +36 fs^2/mm at 800 nm, so a 1.75 mm plate puts about 60 fs^2 into the TRANSMITTED arm only - the two arms of a pump-probe are dispersion-mismatched unless you add a compensating plate. That is a real and commonly overlooked error. AND IT SHOULD BE WEDGED: an unwedged plate gives a back-surface reflection delayed by 2nd cos(theta)/c - a satellite pulse a few picoseconds behind the main one, which shows up as a spurious feature in a pump-probe trace. Check for a wedge when you open it. THE HANDWRITTEN LABEL SAYS "90/20", WHICH CANNOT BE RIGHT - 90 + 20 = 110%. The part number itself carries the 90, so read it as 90:10 (minus a few percent coating loss). Most likely a slip of the pen, possibly confusing it with the adjacent 80:20 part in the same catalogue. PROVENANCE: shipped to UNIV OF CALIF BERKELEY - another item on the Berkeley trail alongside the Bandwidth9 EDFA (MAJ-005), the OZ Optics tapered fibres (ACC-043), the HP 70951A OSA (MAJ-014), stages STG-002/009/010 and wafers WFR-006. Item Name: ACHROMATIC DOUBLET, Ø9 mm, f = 22.5 mm, MgF2 coated - SEALED
Wavelength Range: MgF2 single-layer AR, R average <=1.75% over 400-700 nm
Aperture / Size: Ø9.00 mm (+0/-0.025); centre thickness 4.50 mm, edge 3.58 mm; glasses N-SSK8 / N-SF56; surface quality 40-20
Notes (Function & Operating Range): A FAST LITTLE DOUBLET - f/2.5 at only 9 mm across. NA 0.20 is a good match to 0.22 NA multimode fibre, so the obvious uses here are fibre collimation and launch, collimating a small source, or focusing a few-millimetre beam to a tight spot. WHY A DOUBLET RATHER THAN A SINGLET, and at f/2.5 the usual answer is only half the story: yes the crown/flint pair corrects axial colour, but the extra design freedom is also used to cancel most of the third-order SPHERICAL aberration - and at f/2.5 that is the effect that dominates. A plano-convex singlet this fast is spherical-aberration-limited by a large factor; this doublet gets within a few times the diffraction limit on axis. ORIENTATION MATTERS AND IS EASY TO GET WRONG: for a collimated input, the CROWN element (the more strongly curved convex face, R1) faces the COLLIMATED side and the cemented/flint side faces the focus. Reversed, spherical aberration and coma blow up at f/2.5. For finite-to-finite conjugates near 1:1, use two doublets back to back with the crowns outward. TWO PRACTICAL LIMITS: (1) Ø9 mm does not seat cleanly in a Ø1/2 inch lens tube - it needs a custom cell or a spacer. (2) THE COATING IS A 400-700 nm DESIGN. At 800 nm it is well off its quarter-wave point and reflectance rises, so THIS IS NOT THE RIGHT LENS FOR THE Ti:SAPPHIRE WORK - use a -B coated optic there. On MgF2 generally: a single layer gives about 1.3% per surface at design and 2-3% at the band edges, versus under 0.5% for a good broadband AR and 0.1-0.2% for a V-coat. That is fine for a single element in a throughput-insensitive path, and it matters when you have many surfaces (1.3% over 20 surfaces is 24% loss versus 8%), when ghosts matter (ghost brightness scales as R squared, so about 10x worse than a BBAR), or when launching into a diode - 1.3% back-reflection is only -19 dB return loss.

Item Name: BEAMSPLITTER, 10:90 (R:T), Ø1 inch UV fused silica plate, WEDGED, 45 deg
Part Number: BSN10

Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE VISIBLE-BAND PICK-OFF. Reflects about 10% and passes 90%, so the obvious use is tapping a small monitor beam to a power meter, camera or spectrometer while the bulk of the light goes on to the experiment. The visible-band sibling to FDM-004 (the 800 nm ultrafast 90:10) and FDM-003 (the 1550 nm 50:50). THE 30 ARCMIN WEDGE IS THE POINT, not a manufacturing accident: it walks the back-surface ghost off at a measurable angle so it cannot interfere with the primary reflected beam. Same principle as the wedge prisms in PRI-013. TWO THINGS TO GET RIGHT: (1) THE COATED FACE MUST FACE THE INCOMING BEAM. Flip it and the beam crosses 5 mm of glass before reaching the splitting coating - the reflected arm then exits back through the substrate, doubling its displacement and astigmatism, and the ghost lands where the wedge no longer separates it cleanly. Thorlabs marks the coated side; look for it before mounting. (2) THE RATIO IS POLARISATION DEPENDENT. At 45 degrees any dielectric plate has Rs not equal to Rp, and the quoted 10:90 is the average of the two. For a linearly polarised beam the real ratio shifts with the input polarisation angle. If the split ratio matters to your measurement, fix the polarisation and calibrate at that setting with the power meter (MTR-008). Item Name: CALCITE CRYSTAL BLANK, 10 x 10 x 8 mm - ONE PIECE, sealed
Part Number: No part number. Hand-written label reads 方解石 (calcite), 10x10x8, 1pc
Wavelength Range: Calcite transmits roughly 350 nm to 2.3 um
Aperture / Size: 10 x 10 x 8 mm rectangular block, in a small clear clamshell
Focal Length / Key Spec: Cut angle and orientation NOT MARKED. Calcite is strongly birefringent: no = 1.658, ne = 1.486 at 589 nm, so delta-n is about -0.17
Notes (Function & Operating Range): A BIRDFRINGENT CRYSTAL BLANK, not a nonlinear crystal in the frequency-conversion sense - filed here because that is where the other bulk crystals live. Calcite is THE workhorse birefringent material: the Glan-Taylor polarizers in this catalogue (POL-001/002/003) and the Glan-Laser (POL-008) are all calcite prisms. WHAT A 10 x 10 x 8 mm BLOCK IS FOR: most likely a BEAM DISPLACER or a walk-off plate. With delta-n about 0.17 and the optic axis cut at 45 degrees, calcite separates the ordinary and extraordinary rays by roughly 0.1 x the thickness - so an 8 mm block gives about 0.8 mm of lateral separation between the two orthogonal polarisations, both exiting parallel. That is the standard way to build a polarisation-analysing detection arm where you want BOTH polarisations, side by side, rather than throwing one away as a polarizer does. FLAG - THE CUT IS EVERYTHING AND IT IS NOT MARKED: a beam displacer needs the optic axis at about 45 degrees to the faces; a waveplate blank needs it parallel; a polarizer prism needs a specific wedge. Without knowing the cut you cannot predict what it will do. Look for a scribed axis mark on an edge, or test it: shine an unpolarised beam through and look for TWO output spots (displacer) versus one (axis normal or parallel to the faces). CALCITE HANDLING - IT IS FRAGILE IN A WAY GLASS IS NOT: it is soft (Mohs 3), it CLEAVES readily along rhombohedral planes, and it is damaged by water and dilute acid. Do not drop it, do not clamp it hard, do not clean it with anything aqueous, and keep it in its box. Thermal shock cracks it too.

Item Name: FREE-SPACE FARADAY OPTICAL ISOLATOR, 780 nm, Ø5 mm - SEALED, NEW
Wavelength Range: Centre 780 nm; full range 740-820 nm; tuning range 760-800 nm (rotate the analyser to recover peak isolation)
Aperture / Size: 5 mm clear aperture, Ø4.7 mm max beam; cylindrical housing, 0.18 kg
Focal Length / Key Spec: ISOLATION 35 dB typical at centre; transmission ~90% (NOT CONFIRMED); max power 1.7 W; power density limits 25 W/cm2 blocking, 100 W/cm2 transmission. POLARIZATION-DEPENDENT design
Notes (Function & Operating Range): A ONE-WAY VALVE FOR LIGHT - high transmission forward, about 35 dB attenuation backward. This protects a laser from its own back-reflections, and it is not a luxury: diode lasers and ECDLs at 780 nm are acutely sensitive to feedback. As little as 1e-4 of the output returning into the cavity causes MODE HOPPING, linewidth broadening, frequency pulling, excess amplitude noise, and at worse levels chaotic coherence collapse or physical damage to the diode facet. Every downstream surface - fibre tips, cell windows, AOMs, even a detector face - sends something back. HOW IT WORKS, because the non-reciprocity is the whole trick: input polarizer, then a Faraday rotator (magneto-optic crystal in a permanent axial magnetic field) that rotates the polarisation 45 degrees, then an analyser set at 45 degrees which passes it. The rotation direction is set by the MAGNETIC FIELD, not by the propagation direction - so returning light gets another +45 degrees in the same absolute sense rather than having it undone, arrives at the input polarizer at 90 degrees, and is rejected. A waveplate cannot do this: a waveplate is reciprocal and simply undoes itself on the return trip. THREE PRACTICAL POINTS: (1) IT HAS A DIRECTION. There is an arrow on the housing and the beam must go that way. Installed backwards it still transmits, but you get NO isolation in the direction you care about - you have fitted an expensive pair of polarizers. (2) THE INPUT MUST BE LINEARLY POLARISED AND ALIGNED to the input polarizer. Rotate the isolator body, or put a half-wave plate in front (the FR600HM, MSC-006, would do it). Misalignment costs transmission as cos-squared - it does not cost isolation, so you can quietly throw away most of your power without noticing. (3) RESPECT THE 1.7 W AND THE POWER-DENSITY LIMITS - thermal lensing and depolarisation in the rotator degrade isolation well before anything is damaged. PART NUMBER: IO = free-space optical isolator, 5 = 5 mm aperture, 780 = centre wavelength, VLP = Very Low Power polarizer type (siblings are LP and HP). Still sealed in its bag with hex keys.

Item Name: FRESNEL RHOMB HALF-WAVE RETARDER, MOUNTED, 10 mm CA - SEALED, NEW
Part Number: FR600HM  |  TP04154180  |  Made in USA
Wavelength Range: 400-1550 nm IN A SINGLE PART - visible right through to telecom
Aperture / Size: Clear aperture Ø10.0 mm (+0.0/-0.1); N-BK7; surface quality 20-10 on both faces; cylindrical mount, SM1-threaded (NOT CONFIRMED)
Focal Length / Key Spec: Retardance lambda/2 (180 deg). Accuracy about 2% over 600-1550 nm, 5% max at 400 nm
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE ACHROMATIC HALF-WAVE PLATE - and it is the most broadband retarder in this catalogue by a very wide margin. One part covers 400-1550 nm, which spans essentially every source in the lab from the 405 nm violet line through 800 nm Ti:Sapphire to the 1550 nm telecom bench. WHY IT WORKS WHERE A WAVEPLATE DOES NOT: a birefringent waveplate gets its retardance from delta-n x d / lambda, so the retardance is EXPLICITLY wavelength-dependent - a zero-order quartz half-wave plate is only half-wave at one wavelength and drifts away quickly either side. A Fresnel rhomb instead gets its retardance from the PHASE SHIFT BETWEEN S AND P ON TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION, which depends only on the incidence angle and the refractive index. Since n varies very slowly with wavelength in glass, the retardance is nearly achromatic. Two TIRs at the right angle contribute 90 degrees each, summing to 180. THREE TRADE-OFFS, and the second one bites people: (1) IT IS BIG AND HEAVY - a solid glass block tens of mm long, not a thin plate. It dominates the space in a beam path and does not fit tidily in a cage system. (2) THE OUTPUT BEAM IS LATERALLY OFFSET from the input (parallel, but displaced), because the beam makes two internal reflections. So it is NOT a drop-in replacement for a waveplate in an aligned system - and if you ROTATE it to change the polarisation angle, THE OFFSET BEAM SWEEPS AROUND A CIRCLE. That is the single biggest practical annoyance. Plan the downstream alignment around it. (3) IT IS ANGLE SENSITIVE - the retardance depends on the internal incidence angle, so it needs a well-collimated beam near normal incidence on the entrance face. BEHAVIOUR: exactly like a half-wave plate - linear input at angle theta to the fast axis comes out linear at minus theta, i.e. rotated by 2 theta. Rotate the rhomb 45 degrees and the polarisation flips 90 degrees. Pairs naturally with the isolator (MSC-005) for setting input polarisation, and with the Glan polarizers for a broadband variable attenuator.

Part Number: Stock #32505 (#32-505); label "BS CUBE DICHROIC 25MM TS"; barcode 0100056668

Notes (Function & Operating Range): A GENERAL-PURPOSE VISIBLE 50/50 SPLITTER - illumination pick-offs, autocollimators, camera/eyepiece splits, interferometer arms. The cost is 25 mm of GLASS in the transmitted arm, which means real dispersion, added optical path, spherical aberration in a converging beam, and serious pulse broadening for femtosecond light - so DO NOT put this in the Ti:Sapphire path; use the plate splitters (FDM-004, FDM-005) there. Item Name: CHLOROFORM (trichloromethane), >=99.5%, AMYLENE-STABILISED
Part Number: C2432-2.5L; CAS 67-66-3; Source SHBT5950; PCode 1003890477; contains 100-200 ppm amylenes as stabilizer
Wavelength Range: GHS DANGER - H331 TOXIC IF INHALED, H351 suspected carcinogen, H361d suspected of damaging the unborn child, H372 organ damage (liver/kidney/CNS) on repeated exposure, H302, H315, H319, H336
Aperture / Size: 2.5 L metal can
Focal Length / Key Spec: bp 60.5-61.5 C; mp -63 C; density 1.492 g/mL at 25 C (HEAVIER THAN WATER - it is the lower phase); vapour pressure 160 mmHg at 20 C; nD20 1.445. DOES NOT FLASH - chloroform is NOT flammable
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE SOLVENT FOR THE PC TRANSFER RECIPE - pairs with the polycarbonate (CHM-013) to make the PC/PDMS stamp. See CHM-013 for the recipe. THIS IS THE MOST ACUTELY DANGEROUS CHEMICAL IN THE CATALOGUE. It is worse than NMP (CHM-002), and in a different way: NMP is a reproductive hazard you absorb through skin, chloroform is TOXIC BY INHALATION and a suspected carcinogen, and it evaporates fast (160 mmHg). EXPOSURE LIMITS, which are strikingly low: OSHA is a CEILING of 50 ppm - not a time-weighted average, a ceiling you must never exceed. ACGIH TLV is 10 ppm. NIOSH recommends 2 ppm and treats it as a potential occupational carcinogen. IARC Group 2B, NTP "reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen", California Prop 65 listed for BOTH cancer and reproductive toxicity. FUME HOOD, ALWAYS - there is no version of this that is fine on the open bench. NITRILE GLOVES GIVE ONLY MINUTES of breakthrough against chloroform: treat them as splash protection, change them immediately after any contact, and use laminate (Silver Shield / 4H) for real handling. THE PHOSGENE PROBLEM - THIS IS WHY THE LABEL SAYS "AMYLENES". Chloroform photo-oxidises: light and dissolved oxygen generate CCl3 radicals which react with O2 and collapse to PHOSGENE (COCl2) plus HCl. The reaction is autocatalytic, so it accelerates once started, and it runs faster in a bottle that has been opened (fresh oxygen) and faster in clear glass. Phosgene is a chemical-warfare agent. The 100-200 ppm of AMYLENE (2-methyl-2-butene) is a RADICAL SCAVENGER that stops the chain before phosgene forms. Note what that does NOT mean: amylene does not destroy phosgene once it exists, and it evaporates off (bp 38 C). So amylene-stabilised chloroform has a SHORTER safe life once opened than the ethanol-stabilised kind, which works instead by consuming phosgene at 0.5-1% ethanol. WHY THE AMYLENE GRADE IS NEVERTHELESS THE RIGHT ONE HERE: 1% ethanol is a real cosolvent and a non-solvent for polycarbonate - it hazes or skins a 6% PC dope and leaves residue at the van der Waals interface. At 100-200 ppm with a 38 C boiling point, amylene leaves nothing behind. This is why the 2D community specifies ethanol-free chloroform. STORAGE AND SHELF LIFE: amber container, tightly closed, DARK, cool, ventilated - never in sunlight or near a UV source. Keep away from strong bases, strong oxidisers and reactive metals (Na, K, Li, Mg, Al powder - potentially explosive). Unopened it keeps 1-2 years; ONCE OPENED treat it as good for about 6 months, and for critical film casting more like 1-3 months. WITH A 2.5 L CAN, ALIQUOT INTO A SMALL AMBER WORKING BOTTLE AND KEEP THE MOTHER CAN SEALED - repeatedly opening the big can is what kills it. Never decant used solvent back in. HOW TO TELL IT HAS GONE BAD: a sharp acrid pungent smell instead of the sweet chloroform odour; yellowing; ACIDITY - shake a little with water and test the aqueous layer with pH paper (phosgene hydrolyses to CO2 + 2 HCl). Also unexplained film defects or hazy substrates. Item Name: POLY(BISPHENOL A CARBONATE) (PC), average Mw ~45,000 by GPC - pellets
Wavelength Range: Not classified as hazardous - the product page carries no pictogram, signal word or H-statements. NOT FULLY CONFIRMED (the SDS was unreachable); treat dust or fume from melt processing as an irritant

Focal Length / Key Spec: GLASS TRANSITION Tg = 150 C. Density 1.2 g/mL at 25 C; nD20 1.585. Thermal decomposition onset ~440-480 C. Soluble in CHLOROFORM (excellent), dichloromethane, THF, dioxane, NMP; NOT soluble in alcohols, water, aliphatics or acetone; and NOT soluble in ANISOLE
Notes (Function & Operating Range): THE SECOND TRANSFER RECIPE. With the chloroform (CHM-012) this gives the lab a PC/PDMS stamp alongside the PPC/anisole one it already had (CHM-003 + CHM-001) - and the two are complementary, not redundant. THE PC RECIPE (Zomer et al., Appl. Phys. Lett. 105, 013101, 2014): 6 wt% PC in chloroform. DO NOT TRY TO SPIN-COAT IT - the original authors found spin coating difficult. Instead DRIP the solution onto a glass microscope slide, lay a second slide on top and immediately SLIDE IT OFF sideways, leaving a uniform film; air-dry about 15 minutes. Lift the dried film off with adhesive tape and drape it over the PDMS block, tape acting as the frame. PICK UP at 60-90 C, then switch the heater off and retract while cooling. RELEASE at about 150 C to melt the PC onto the target. Dissolve the PC off in chloroform, roughly 10 minutes. CRITICAL POINT ABOUT THE STAMP, AND IT EXPLAINS THE WHOLE ODD PROCEDURE: the PC film is cast on GLASS and only then transferred to the PDMS. THE CHLOROFORM MUST NEVER TOUCH THE PDMS. Chloroform swells PDMS by about 39% (Whitesides swelling ratio S = 1.39, among the worst solvents tested) - casting directly onto the stamp would destroy it. The PDMS here is purely a compliant mechanical backing, chemically isolated from the solvent. This is the opposite of the PPC recipe, where anisole IS spun straight onto the PDMS. WHICH RECIPE TO USE - the deciding factor is TEMPERATURE BUDGET: PC (Tg 150 C): pick up at 60-110 C, release at 150-180 C. Choose it for RELIABLE hBN PICKUP - PC grips hBN better and is the workhorse for hBN-encapsulated graphene; for MANY-LAYER STACKS where each pickup needs a robust film; when you want intermediate hot steps mid-stack; and for the cleanest final interface, since PC dissolves off more completely. PPC (Tg 35-40 C): pick up at ~40 C, release at ~90 C. Choose it for THERMALLY FRAGILE OR AIR-SENSITIVE MATERIALS - CrI3, black phosphorus, MnBi2Te4, thin superconductors, organics - because the whole cycle tops out at 90 C rather than 180 C; for release onto pre-patterned electrodes or flexible substrates; and for glovebox work. Rule of thumb: PC = high temperature, high yield, hBN-first, cleanest stacks. PPC = low temperature, delicate materials. WHY Mw ~45,000 SPECIFICALLY: it is the deliberate middle. At 45k a 6% chloroform dope is fluid enough to spread between two slides into a uniform micron film; a 100k+ PC at 6% is stringy and gels. It is also comfortably above the entanglement threshold so the film is self-supporting and does not tear on pickup, yet low enough to flow and detach cleanly at 150-180 C. Very high Mw makes release sluggish and drags the stack; very low Mw gives brittle films and oligomeric residue. This is the standard grade for the recipe. Note PC is AMORPHOUS - the "Tm 267 C" some datasheets list is a formality, there is no sharp melt. It softens through 150 C and melt-processes at 260-300 C. Keep the bottle out of direct sunlight as the label says.

A watt of visible light coming out of a diverging fibre cone will damage an eye instantly, will burn skin, and will ignite dark plastic or paper at close range. NEVER look into the connector, powered or not, and NEVER put a fibre inspection scope on a fibre that might be live. READING THE THREE-WAVELENGTH LABEL, which confuses everyone: only ONE of those bands comes out. Sapphire is an OPSL - optically pumped semiconductor laser - so an 808 nm diode (the 0.79-0.82 um line) pumps a semiconductor chip which lases around 1.04-1.16 um inside the cavity, and an intracavity doubling crystal halves that to the 0.52-0.57 um green you actually use. The 20 mW and 200 mW figures are leakage ratings for the internal fields, not outputs. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: green-only laser goggles are NOT sufficient if a fibre or splice ever fails - you need eyewear that also blocks ~808 nm and ~1100 nm, both invisible. WAVELENGTH: the '548' tab is almost certainly 548 nm. That is NOT a Coherent catalogue wavelength (the published Sapphire list is 458, 488, 514, 532, 552, 561, 568, 588, 594), so this is a CUSTOM OEM build - OPSL lets Coherent pick any wavelength. Be careful: the 532nm patch cords lying with them are NOT matched to the heads. PROVENANCE - NOT CONFIRMED: 'Titan' appears in no Coherent literature at all; it reads as a customer programme name. A published teardown of a visually identical assembly (two Sapphire heads, OEM LPX-class controllers, common baseplate, PM fibre spliced to a Diamond E-2000 shuttered pigtail) identifies it as coming from a PacBio Sequel DNA sequencer, and that unit was marked 'Sapphire 548-300 FPT FT' - 548 nm, 300 mW. SO THE 1.3 W ON THE LABEL MAY BE A FAMILY CEILING RATHER THAN THIS UNIT'S POWER. Treat it as 1.3 W until measured. TO RUN ONE ON THE BENCH: +10.8-15 VDC (12 V nominal) at >60 W, low ripple; RS-232 at 19200 8N1; 10-pin Molex Micro-Fit carrying supply, interlock and keyswitch. The gold heatsink block is NOT optional - the baseplate must stay below 50 C. The driver boards ARE the controllers, so no separate Coherent controller is needed, but the teardown found the head will talk serial and still emit NOTHING with the programme-specific daughter board removed. Fibre minimum bend radius 50 mm - a tight bend on a watt-class fibre is a burn and fire point, not just a loss. NOT RECORDED: measured output power, whether both heads work, the exact daughter-board revision, and whether a suitable 12 V supply exists in the lab.

Notes (Function & Operating Range): SILICON-ON-INSULATOR, and the layer stack is the whole story: DEVICE LAYER 60 +/- 1 um, BURIED OXIDE (BOX) 2 um +/- 5%, HANDLE 450 +/- 15 um. Type/orientation P/B (boron-doped p-type), (100). BOTH device and handle are 0.001-0.005 ohm-cm, i.e. HEAVILY DOPED AND HIGHLY CONDUCTIVE - this is not high-resistivity SOI. WHAT THAT COMBINATION IS FOR: a 60 um device layer is far too thick for photonics or for 2D-material substrates and is the signature of MEMS / bulk micromachining - you etch all the way through the 60 um by DRIE and the 2 um buried oxide acts as the etch stop, releasing a suspended structure. The low resistivity means the silicon is being used as a conductor (electrodes, electrostatic actuators, through-silicon contacts), not as a low-loss optical or RF medium. If anyone is planning to use these as a photonics or RF substrate, that is a mistake: 0.001-0.005 ohm-cm silicon is lossy. IMPORTANT - THIS IS NOT THE 2D-MATERIAL SUBSTRATE. The oxide here is BURIED under 60 um of silicon, so it gives you NO optical contrast for finding flakes. For exfoliation you still need the 285 nm or 90 nm thermal-oxide wafers (see the other WFR entries). Do not let anyone grab these by mistake. KEEP THE BAG SEALED until needed - it is an ESD/moisture barrier bag and once opened the wafers start collecting particles. 150 mm is 6 inch, so check your chucks and carriers actually take 6 inch before planning around them.
